['Interestingly enough, Marx, who had learned Russian in order to study Russian economic conditions, carefully read
Statism and Anarchy.
Sometime in 1874–75 he went through the work and made lengthy extracts and notes. His own comments on it are few but revealing. His chief criticism of Bakunin was that he did not pay enough attention to the economic preconditions of revolution. “Will,” Marx complained, “not economic conditions, is the basis of his social revolution.” There was much to be said for this judgment. What Marx did not perceive so clearly was that precisely the opposite criticism might be leveled against him. His only response to Bakunin’s warning that socialism might produce a new ruling elite was to reiterate confidently that once economic conditions were changed and class rule came to an end, the state and all relations of political authority would necessarily disappear.[31] He would not entertain the possibility that political domination was a product of will, and not solely of economic conditions, and that the former might persist even after the latter had been transformed.

It is in the attack on Marx that the literary artistry of
Statism and Anarchy
reveals itself. The discussion of Marx and his views appears only in the last third of the book. By the time Bakunin gets to Marx, however, he has so identified the Germans with “statism” that Marx’s political outlook takes on a truly sinister cast. In the context which
Statism and Anarchy
has created, Marx becomes a kind of socialist Bismarck, promoting pan-German hegemony by other means. Whatever the fairness or accuracy of such a depiction – and it should be kept in mind that Marx, Lassalle, and the new German Social-Democratic Party, all of whom Bakunin lumps together, actually held different views on many issues – it is the product of a degree of literary skill for which Bakunin is rarely given credit.', 'A closely related issue concerned the structure and organization of the International itself. If components of the International were to engage in contemporary political life, the organization required a certain amount of centralization in order to provide information, support, and coordination, and thus, at the very least, an enhanced role for the General Council. To the anarchists, the International must serve as a direct model for the new society, a microcosm of the free future order. Therefore they envisioned it as a true federation, with local sections enjoying the greatest possible degree of autonomy. Thus the debate over the powers of the General Council (and hence of Marx, who dominated it) was really a debate over basic issues of the International’s strategy and objectives.

Bakunin contended that if the Marxists attempted to work through the state to achieve their ends, there could be only two results: either they would be drawn into the parliamentary system and would become indistinguishable from the bourgeois parties; or, if they ever came to power, they would form a new ruling elite over the masses. In twentieth-century terms, the result would be either West European Social Democracy or Leninism–Stalinism. Bakunin spelled out the second possibility in the most remarkable passage in
Statism and Anarchy,
his description of what a Marxist “dictatorship of the proletariat” would look like. Brief as it is, it is a chilling picture of Stalin’s Russia some sixty years before the fact, and a prophecy of the rise of the “new class” long before Milovan Djilas made the term famous.', 'Equally repellent, though less marked in this work than in some others, is Bakunin’s anti-Semitism, which often appeared as a corollary to his anti-Germanism. Again, it is in part a weapon in his war against Marx. Not only was Marx himself Jewish as well as German, but some of those who helped him in his campaign against Bakunin were also Jewish. Bakunin’s anti-Semitism, however, long antedated his conflict with Marx. It may be argued that such sentiments, however distasteful, do not negate Bakunin’s anarchist principles.[29] It may also be argued that those principles are somehow deficient if even one so passionately committed to them was unable to surmount crude ethnic prejudices. The most that can be said for Bakunin is that he was hardly unique in this regard. In France, for example, at least until the Dreyfus affair, socialist and anarchist writers and artists frequently employed stereotypical anti-Semitic images of the Jew as capitalist or banker, or simply as a crude synonym for “bourgeois.”[30] It should be noted also that Bakunin’s consistent (though not uncritical) support and defense of the Poles – in regard to whom so many otherwise liberal Russians had a moral blind spot – was a remarkable example of adherence to principle.

The second major theme of
Statism and Anarchy
is its critique of Marxism. To the Marxists, the proletariat’s participation in the political life of its respective nations seemed an effective way of pursuing the class struggle and ultimately achieving the supremacy of the proletariat and the elimination of the state. To the anarchists, however, any participation in “bourgeois politics” was inherently corrupting. One could fight the enemy or one could join the enemy, but one could not do both. To expect to use political methods to abolish political domination was a dangerous delusion.', 'In opposition to both statism and Marxism, Bakunin presents in broad outline the principles of “anarchy,” as he calls what we would today term anarchism, and the anarchist society of the future. In the most general terms it can be said that each of the three competing political ideologies of the nineteenth century, liberalism, socialism, and anarchism, took its stand primarily on one element of the French Revolution’s trinity, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity. Anarchism joined socialism in rejecting nineteenth-century parliamentarism, or “bourgeois democracy,” as a narrow conception of liberty which could be enjoyed only by the propertied classes as long as economic inequality prevailed. The anarchist critique of liberalism added little to that of the socialists, and the pages of
Statism and Anarchy
dealing with this subject are perhaps the least original – and, in retrospect, some of the most short-sighted – in the book. response:
According to Bakunin in "Statism and Anarchy," the state is an instrument of oppression used by one class to dominate another. He argues that any participation of the working class in state politics is inherently corrupting and that using political methods to abolish political domination is a dangerous delusion. Bakunin contends that the state will not wither away on its own but will be replaced by a federation of autonomous communities.

In contrast, Marx in "Critique of the Gotha Programme" states that the state will dissolve of itself and disappear as soon as the proletariat uses it to keep down its enemies. Marx suggests that the state is a transitional institution and that the term "people’s state" is nonsense. He proposes that the term "Gemeinwesen" (commonalty) be used instead of "state" and emphasizes that a socialist society should aim for a realm of equality rather than abolishing all class distinctions.

These views reflect a fundamental difference in their understanding of the state's role and eventual fate in the transition to a socialist society. While Bakunin sees the state as an enduring and potentially corrupting institution, Marx views it as a temporary tool that will naturally dissolve with the establishment of a socialist order.
reference: Bakunin argues in Statism and Anarchy that all states, even democratic ones or Marx's proposed popular state, inherently represent elite governance from above downward by a privileged minority. In contrast, Marx (in Critique of the Gotha Programme, as articulated by Engels) defines the state as a temporary, transitional instrument used during revolution solely to suppress political enemies by force. While Bakunin views state power as inherently oppressive and anti-popular, Marx contends that the state is utilized for forcible repression during revolutionary struggle, and that the state as such ceases to exist once true freedom becomes possible.

He expected that with the abolition of the right of inheritance, private ownership would disappear within a generation, to be gradually superseded by workers’ productive associations. He feared that an immediate massive expropriation might find the workers unprepared to take control. This would leave the way open for a bureaucratic administrative apparatus. It would lead to a worse evil, namely, the restoration of authoritarian institutions. Based on the provided context, there are several key differences between John Stuart Mill's harm principle and Mikhail Bakunin's concept of individual freedom as outlined in the Revolutionary Catechism:

1. **Scope of Freedom**:
   - **Mill**: Mill's concept of individual freedom is more narrowly focused on the freedom of thought and expression, and the freedom to act as one sees fit as long as it does not harm others. He emphasizes the importance of individual development and diversity.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin's concept of individual freedom is more broadly defined, encompassing not just freedom of thought and action, but also the freedom to participate in collective decision-making and the freedom from oppressive institutions. He emphasizes the interdependence of individual and collective freedom.

2. **Role of Society**:
   - **Mill**: Mill acknowledges that society has a legitimate role in limiting individual freedom to prevent harm to others, but he believes this should be minimal and based on the harm principle.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin sees society as inherently oppressive and advocates for the destruction of all oppressive institutions. He believes that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state and the establishment of a society organized by workers' associations.

3. **Nature of Freedom**:
   - **Mill**: Mill's freedom is primarily about the absence of external constraints on individual actions, as long as they do not harm others.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin's freedom is more about the ability to participate in the collective decision-making process and to live in a society without hierarchical structures or oppressive institutions.

4. **Purpose of Freedom**:
   - **Mill**: Mill's purpose of freedom is to allow for the fullest development of individual potential and to promote a diverse and vibrant society.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin's purpose of freedom is to create a society where individuals can live freely and cooperatively, without the constraints of a state or other oppressive structures.

In summary, while both Mill and Bakunin advocate for individual freedom, their conceptions differ significantly in terms of the scope of freedom, the role of society, and the ultimate goals of freedom. Mill's view is more individualistic and limited by the harm principle, whereas Bakunin's view is more collective and aims at the abolition of oppressive structures.
reference: Mill's harm principle in On Liberty asserts that society is only warranted in interfering with an individual's liberty to prevent harm to others, holding that a person's own physical or moral good is never a sufficient reason for coercion. Conversely, Bakunin rejects the notion in the Revolutionary Catechism that individual freedom is limited or bounded by the freedom of others, maintaining instead that freedom expands through the liberty of fellow human beings. While Mill establishes a negative boundary based on self-protection against external interference, Bakunin frames freedom as an interdependent social condition requiring absolute equality and mutual recognition.

John Stuart Mill's account of women's moral education in "The Subjection of Women" and Karl Marx's analysis of female industrial labor in "Capital, Volume 1" present different perspectives on the treatment of women, but both highlight the constraints placed on women.

In "The Subjection of Women," Mill argues that women's moral education is shaped to make them submissive and focused on serving others, rather than developing self-will or self-control. He states that women are brought up to believe that their ideal character is one of submission and yielding to the control of others. Mill criticizes this education, seeing it as a means to maintain women's subordination.

In contrast, Marx's analysis in "Capital, Volume 1" focuses on the exploitation of women and children in industrial labor. He describes how the capitalist system degrades women and children through the exploitation of their labor, leading to moral and intellectual desolation. Marx notes that the education clauses in the Factory Acts, intended to provide education for child workers, are undermined by the capitalist system, which prioritizes profit over the well-being of workers.

While Mill criticizes the moral education of women as a means of maintaining their subordination, Marx critiques the industrial system for exploiting women and children, leading to a similar outcome of degradation and desolation. Both authors highlight the negative impacts of societal structures on women, though they approach the issue from different angles: one focusing on the moral and intellectual development, and the other on the economic exploitation.

*** Introduction

These “Letters to a Frenchman” were not actually addressed to anyone in particular, but were merely the form the author used to indicate the informality and personal quality of what he had to say.

This long extract naturally divides itself into three distinct sections: a)
General Problems of the Social Revolution
, with special emphasis on the organization of the peasants in relation to the urban working class in predominantly agrarian countries, capitalist war between states, and civil war; b)
The Revolutionary Temper and Its Matrix
; c)
A Critique of the German Social-Democratic Program
.

His
Letters to a Frenchman
are among the most important of Bakunin’s writings. For it is in this major work that Bakunin made his unique contributions to the theory and practice of revolution. It was written during the stormy period of the Franco-Prussian War when France faced certain defeat. The government of Napoleon III had collapsed and the succeeding provisional republican government was hopelessly demoralized. The French armies were in full retreat and the Prussian troops were at the gates of Paris. It was in the midst of this crisis that Bakunin developed ideas which have since become the watchwords of libertarian revolutionary movements and to which even the authoritarians still pay lip service — ideas such as turning the wars between states into civil wars for the Social Revolution; the people-in-arms fighting a guerrilla war to repulse a foreign army and simultaneously defending the revolution against its domestic enemies; all power to the grass-roots organizations spontaneously created by the revolution; a federalist alternative to centralized statist revolution-by-decree, among others.', 'Bakunin’s had confidence in the revolutionary capabilities of the peasants, and he worked out ways of winning them over to the side of the revolution, with particular emphasis on establishing harmonious relations between the peasants and the more sophisticated urban workers. As in all his other writings on revolution, he reiterates his views on the relation between the vanguard organization and the masses. While fully appreciating the importance of the economic situation in revolution, Bakunin nevertheless attached equal weight to the will, the revolutionary consciousness of the people. The section on
The Revolutionary Temper and Its Matrix
occupies a key place in Bakunin’s revolutionary ideology.

*** General Problems of the Social Revolution

I have already shown that France cannot be saved ... by the State. But outside the parasitic, artificial institution of State, a nation consists only of its people; consequently,
France can be saved only by the immediate, non-partisan action of the people,
by a mass uprising of all the French people, spontaneously organized from the bottom upward, a war of destruction, a merciless war to the death.

When a nation of thirty-eight million people rises to defend itself, determined to destroy everything and ready even to sacrifice lives and possessions rather than submit to slavery, no army in the world, however powerful, however well organized and equipped with the most extraordinary weapons, will be able to conquer it.

Everything depends on the ability of the French people to make such an effort. To what extent have blandishments of bourgeois civilization affected their revolutionary capacities?

Have such factors rendered them incapable of summoning up the requisite heroism and primitive tenacity, do they prefer peace at the price of freedom, or freedom at the cost of immense privations? Do they still retain at least some of the natural strength and primitive energy which makes a nation powerful?', 'Labor employed by the State — such is the fundamental, principle of authoritarian communism, of state socialism. The State, having become the sole proprietor — at the end of a period of transition necessary for allowing society to pass, without too great dislocation, from the present organization of bourgeois privilege to the future organization of official equality for all — the State will then become the only banker, capitalist, organizer, and director of all national labor, and the distributor of all its products. Such is the ideal the fundamental principle of modern communism.

\xa0

The book was widely circulated by 1872 it was translated into several languages and published throughout Europe and the United States.
The first address was delivered on July 23rd, 1870, five days after the beginning of the Franco-Prussian War. The Civil War in France
was originally published by Marx as only the third address (here comprising Chapters 3 through 6) separated into four chapters. In 1891, on the 20th anniversary of the Paris Commune, Engels put together a new collection of the work. Also, Engels 1891 introduction has been separated into two parts: an introduction (below) and a postscript.', 'Marx to Ludwig Kugelmann
In Hanover
[London] April 17, 1871
Dear Kugelmann
Your letter duly received. Just at present I have my hands full. Hence only a few words.
... How you can compare petty-bourgeois demonstrations
à la
13 June
[1]
,
1849, etc., with the present struggle in Paris is quite
incomprehensible to me.
World history would indeed be very easy to make, if the struggle were
taken up only on condition of infallibly favorable chances. It would,
on the other hand, be a very mystical nature, if “accidents” played no
part. These accidents themselves fall naturally into the general course
of development and are compensated again by other accidents. But
acceleration and delay are very dependent upon such “accidents,” which
included the "accident" of the character of those who at first stand at
the head of the movement.
The decisive, unfavorable “accident” this time is by no means to be
found in the general conditions of French society, but in the presence
of the Prussians in France and their position right before Paris. Of
this the Parisians were well aware. But of this, the bourgeois
canaille
of Versailles were also well aware. Precisely for that
reason they presented the Parisians with the alternative of taking up
the fight of succumbing without a struggle. In the latter case, the
demoralization of the working class against the capitalist class and its
state has entered upon a new phase with the struggle in paris. Whatever
the immediate results may be, a new point of departure of world-historic
importance has been gained. ...

According to the provided context, Karl Marx's description of the Paris Commune in "The Civil War in France" contrasts with Mikhail Bakunin's revolutionary stance in "Letters to a Frenchman on the Present Crisis" in several ways:

1. **Structure and Organization**:
   - **Marx**: Marx describes the Paris Commune as having a mixed composition, with a majority of Blanquists and a minority of International Working Men's Association members, including adherents of the Proudhon school of socialism. He notes that the Blanquists were primarily socialist by revolutionary and proletarian instinct, while only a few had attained greater clarity through Vaillant, who was familiar with German scientific socialism.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin, on the other hand, emphasizes the importance of the spontaneous actions of the people and the grassroots organizations. He advocates for a federalist alternative to centralized statist revolution-by-decree, suggesting that power should reside with the grass-roots organizations spontaneously created by the revolution.

2. **Role of the State**:
   - **Marx**: Marx views the Paris Commune as a form of state power, albeit a more democratic and workers' state. He notes that the Commune was a product of the struggle against the state and the capitalist class, but still acknowledges its structural limitations.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin is critical of any form of state power, advocating for a stateless society. He emphasizes the need for a decentralized, federated system where power is distributed among the people and their local organizations, rather than centralized in a state apparatus.

3. **Revolutionary Consciousness**:
   - **Marx**: Marx acknowledges that the French workers had lost their revolutionary impetus and were influenced by abstract theories rather than their concrete living experiences. He sees the need for a reawakening of revolutionary consciousness among the working class.
   - **Bakunin**: Bakunin places a strong emphasis on the revolutionary consciousness and capabilities of the people, particularly the peasants and urban workers. He believes in the spontaneous uprising of the masses and the importance of maintaining their revolutionary spirit and will.

In summary, while both Marx and Bakunin recognize the importance of the working class in revolution, their visions differ significantly in terms of the structural organization of the revolution and the role of the state. Marx sees the Paris Commune as a step towards a more democratic state, whereas Bakunin advocates for a stateless, decentralized, and federated system.
reference: In The Civil War in France, Marx praises the Paris Commune as a functional working body that combined executive and legislative functions, composed of municipal councillors chosen by universal suffrage who were accountable and revocable at short terms. On the other hand, Bakunin insists in Letters to a Frenchman on the Present Crisis that a true revolution requires the complete destruction and abolition of the political and legal state and the principle of authority altogether. While Marx endorses the Commune's new institutional form of working-class governance, Bakunin maintains that establishing any state apparatus—even a provisional one—serves as the center of reaction rather than freedom.

response:
John Stuart Mill justifies extending the suffrage by arguing that it ensures the representation of all individuals, not just the majority. He states that when the vote of the elector is determined by their own will, their position is similar to that of a member of Parliament, and thus, publicity is indispensable. Mill believes that extending the suffrage to all men, and eventually to all women, would ensure that various classes and groups have a voice in the legislative process, allowing them to have a say in matters that directly affect them.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin's assessment of political obedience, as seen in his Letter to La Liberté, is highly critical. Bakunin opposes the idea of the State and the government as a necessary evil. He views the existence or stability of the State as a threat to freedom and believes that the government is fundamentally of religious origin, with the idea of obeying authority derived from religious teachings. Bakunin advocates for the abolition of artificial, privileged, legal, and official influences, rather than extending the suffrage to ensure representation.

Bakunin's view is that political obedience and participation in the State's mechanisms, such as universal suffrage, would corrupt the proletariat and perpetuate the establishment. He fears that workers' participation in bourgeois politics would undermine their revolutionary goals and the establishment of a truly free society.
reference: In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill defends political inclusion by arguing that when any class is excluded from sovereign power, its specific interests are inevitably overlooked or misinterpreted by ruling groups. In contrast, Bakunin asserts in his Letter to La Liberté that representative government is a fiction, because citizens do not obey laws they created themselves, but rather laws enacted in their name by a governing minority. While Mill views enfranchisement as an essential protection against class neglect, Bakunin characterizes compliance with representative legislation as voluntary servitude to a ruling elite.

According to the provided context, Bakunin and Marx have different strategic focuses regarding property and inheritance.

Bakunin emphasizes the abolition of the right of inheritance as a means to achieve economic, social, and political equality. He argues that the right of inheritance perpetuates class distinctions and exploitation, and that it must be abolished to achieve the emancipation of labor. Bakunin sees the abolition of inheritance as a necessary step towards the establishment of collective labor and property, and the creation of a new international world based on freedom and equality.

In contrast, Marx's focus in the Manifesto is on the abolition of bourgeois property, which he sees as the final and most complete expression of a class-based society. Marx argues that the abolition of private property is a distinctive feature of communism, but he does not specifically mention the right of inheritance. Instead, he discusses the historical development of property relations and how they have changed over time.

Therefore, while both authors advocate for the abolition of certain forms of property, Bakunin's emphasis is more directly on the right of inheritance, whereas Marx's focus is on bourgeois property more broadly. Bakunin sees the abolition of inheritance as a key step towards a more equitable society, while Marx's critique of property is part of a broader analysis of the capitalist mode of production.
reference: In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels summarize communist theory as the abolition of modern bourgeois private property, which they identify as the ultimate system of class exploitation and appropriation. Conversely, Bakunin argues in the Report of the Commission on the Question of Inheritance that the right of inheritance is the primary legal mechanism that perpetuates class divisions and separates capital from labor. While Marx and Engels prioritize directly eliminating bourgeois private property as a mode of production, Bakunin focuses on abolishing the right of inheritance as the key prerequisite for dismantling social inequality and class privileges.

Friends and enemies know that this man was great in thought, will, persistent energy; they know also with what lofty contempt he looked down upon wealth, rank, glory, all the wretched ambitions which most human beings are base enough to entertain. A Russian gentleman related by marriage to the highest nobility of the empire, he was one of the first to enter that intrepid society of rebels who were able to release themselves from traditions, prejudices, race and class interests, and set their own comfort at naught. Government by science is becoming as impossible as that of divine right, wealth, or brute force. All powers are henceforth to be submitted to pitiless criticism. Men in whom the sentiment of equality is born suffer themselves no longer to be governed; they learn to govern themselves. In precipitating from the heights of the heavens him from whom all power is reputed to descend, societies unseat also all those who reigned in his name. Such is the revolution now in progress. States are breaking up to give place to a new order, in which, as Bakunin was fond of saying, “human justice will be substituted for divine justice.” If it is allowable to cite any one name from those of the revolutionists who have taken part in this immense work of renovation, there is not one that may be singled out with more justice than that of Michael Bakunin.

** I

Who are right, the idealists or the materialists? The question once stated in this way, hesitation becomes impossible. Undoubtedly the idealists are wrong and the materialists right. Bakunin never had the time necessary to finish all the tasks he undertook. One work was not completed when others were already under way. “My life itself is a fragment,” he said to those who criticized his writings. Nevertheless, the readers of “God and the State” certainly will not regret that Bakunin’s memoir, incomplete though it be, has been published. The questions discussed in it are treated decisively and with a singular vigor of logic. Rightly addressing himself only to his honest opponents, Bakunin demonstrates to them the emptiness of their belief in that divine authority on which all temporal authorities are founded; he proves to them the purely human genesis of all governments; finally, without stopping to discuss those bases of the State already condemned by public morality, such as physical superiority, violence, nobility, wealth, he does justice to the theory which would entrust science with the government of societies. Based on the provided context, John Stuart Mill's foundational criterion for morality in Utilitarianism and Mikhail Bakunin's definition of moral action in God and the State have some key differences:

1. **Mill's Utilitarianism**:
   - Mill defines the ultimate criterion of right and wrong as the greatest happiness principle. He states that actions are morally right if they promote the greatest happiness for the greatest number.
   - Mill acknowledges that utilitarianism can be applied with varying degrees of strictness, but argues that it provides a tangible and intelligible way to decide moral differences.
   - Mill emphasizes that utilitarianism does not require that the sole motive of all actions be a feeling of duty. He notes that actions can be morally right even if done from other motives, as long as the rule of duty does not condemn them.

2. **Bakunin's God and the State**:
   - Bakunin critiques the idea of divine authority and the notion that governments are founded on divine right.
   - He argues that all governments are of human genesis and that the idea of entrusting science with the governance of societies is flawed. He suggests that even if such a system were possible, it would likely lead to the same follies and crimes as existing governments.
   - Bakunin advocates for a society where people govern themselves, rejecting the idea of a state or government based on any form of authority, divine or otherwise.

In summary, while Mill's Utilitarianism focuses on the greatest happiness principle as the criterion for morality, Bakunin's work emphasizes the rejection of all forms of authority, including divine authority, and advocates for a self-governing society. Mill's approach is more pragmatic and flexible, allowing for a variety of motives, whereas Bakunin's is more radical and absolute in its rejection of established authority structures.

In contrast, Bakunin emphasizes autonomous volition in God and the State, arguing that true morality and human dignity consist in performing good actions freely because one conceives and loves them, rather than out of command or utility calculations. While Mill evaluates morality based on consequential outcomes of happiness and pain reduction, Bakunin grounds morality in voluntary internal motivation free from external authority.

response:
According to John Stuart Mill in "Principles of Political Economy," the right of bequest, or gift after death, is part of the idea of private property, but the right of inheritance, as distinguished from bequest, is not necessarily a consequence of this principle. Mill suggests that the property of individuals who have made no disposition of it during their lifetime should pass first to their children, and failing them, to the nearest relations. However, he sees no reason why collateral inheritance should exist at all and proposes that, in cases of intestacy, the property should escheat to the state.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin in "On the Question of the Right of Inheritance" argues for the abolition of the right of inheritance. He believes that if the right of inheritance is not abolished, it will perpetuate individual property, which has been voted to be transformed into collective property. Bakunin emphasizes that the right of inheritance must be abolished to prevent the legal sanctioning of individual property and to ensure that the revolution's goals are not undermined by the preservation of individual property rights.

Thus, while Mill sees the right of bequest as part of private property but is open to the state taking property in cases of intestacy, Bakunin advocates for the complete abolition of the right of inheritance to align with the goals of collective property.
reference: In Principles of Political Economy, Mill distinguishes between the right of bequest (which he includes in the idea of private property) and the right of intestate inheritance, arguing that passing property to collateral relatives is not an essential consequence of private property rights. In contrast, Bakunin takes a far more radical position in On the Question of the Right of Inheritance, demanding the total abolition of all inheritance rights because they serve as the foundational legal sanction for private property, class division, and the political state. While Mill seeks to limit unearned family transfers while preserving individual bequest, Bakunin targets the complete elimination of inheritance as a necessary step toward social liquidation.

Here's a comparison of the two perspectives:

### Mikhail Bakunin's Perspective on State Security

1. **Critique of the State**: Bakunin was a fierce critic of the state, viewing it as an instrument of oppression and a means of maintaining class domination. He believed that the state inherently serves the interests of the ruling class and is a barrier to true freedom and equality.

2. **Anarchism**: Bakunin advocated for a form of anarchism, which seeks to abolish the state entirely. He believed that the state is a tool of the few to control the many and that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state.

3. **Security and Freedom**: Bakunin argued that security and freedom are not mutually exclusive but are in fact contradictory. He believed that the state's security measures are inherently oppressive and that true security can only be achieved through the collective self-organization of the people.

4. **Mutual Aid**: Bakunin emphasized the importance of mutual aid and cooperation among individuals and communities. He believed that social bonds and mutual aid could provide the necessary security and stability without the need for a coercive state.

### John Stuart Mill's Perspective on Equal Social Relations

1. **Utilitarianism**: Mill's utilitarianism posits that the rightness of an action is determined by its consequences, specifically by the amount of happiness or utility it produces. He believed that the state should aim to maximize overall happiness.

2. **Equal Social Relations**: Mill advocated for equal social relations, particularly in his work "Utilitarianism." He argued that the state should promote equal opportunities and fair treatment for all individuals, ensuring that no one is unfairly disadvantaged.

3. **Liberalism and Individual Rights**: While Mill did not advocate for the complete abolition of the state, he did support a limited state that protects individual rights and promotes social welfare. He believed that the state should intervene to correct inequalities and ensure that the happiness of the majority is not compromised by the actions of the few.

4. **Social Justice**: Mill's utilitarianism includes a strong emphasis on social justice. He argued that the state should work to create a society where the happiness of all individuals is considered, and that inequalities should be addressed to ensure that the least advantaged are not left behind.

### Comparison

1. **Role of the State**:

2. **Social Relations**:

3. **Security**:
   - **Bakunin**: Sees security as a product of mutual aid and collective self-organization, not the state.
   - **Mill**: Sees security as a product of a limited state that protects individual rights and promotes social welfare.

4. **Philosophical Foundations**:
   - **Bakunin**: Grounded in anarchism and a critique of state power.
   - **Mill**: Grounded in utilitarianism and a belief in the state's role in promoting the greatest happiness.

In summary, while both thinkers advocate for a more equitable society, they differ significantly in their views on the role of the state and the means by which social relations can be improved. Bakunin sees the state as an obstacle to freedom and equality, while Mill sees it as a necessary but limited institution that can help achieve these goals.

The anarchist critique of liberalism added little to that of the socialists, and the pages of

Karl Marx's analysis of the French state bureaucracy in "The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte" and Mikhail Bakunin's critique of the state in "Statism and Anarchy" present contrasting views on the nature and role of the state.

Marx views the state bureaucracy as an instrument of class rule. He notes that under different regimes, the state machinery served the interests of the ruling class, whether it was the bourgeoisie or, in the case of the second Bonaparte, the peasantry. Marx argues that the state under the second Bonaparte had become independent of civil society, representing the interests of the small-holding peasants. He sees the state as a tool for the bourgeoisie to maintain class rule, and the rise of Bonapartism as a result of the decline of small-holding property and the need for a centralized state structure.

In contrast, Bakunin's critique of the state in "Statism and Anarchy" is more radical. He opposes any form of state, including what he sees as the socialist state advocated by Marx. Bakunin argues that the state is inherently statist and authoritarian, and that any participation in state politics by the working class would corrupt them. He warns that the state might be used by a new ruling elite, even if it initially claims to represent the proletariat. Bakunin's critique is based on the belief that the state is a tool of oppression and that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state.

While Marx acknowledges the state's role in class rule and its potential for independence, Bakunin sees the state as an irredeemable institution that must be completely abolished. Marx's analysis is more nuanced, recognizing the state's historical development and its potential to change, whereas Bakunin's critique is more absolute and focused on the state's inherent oppressive nature.
reference: In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, Marx analyzes the French executive state power as a massive bureaucratic and military parasitic body that historical development centralized and expanded to enmesh civil society. In Statism and Anarchy, Bakunin similarly characterizes the state as a dominant power soaring above society, but concludes that any state fundamentally necessitates domination and slavery, whether open or camouflaged. Both thinkers diagnose the modern centralized state machinery as a suffocating, parasitic force, though Marx analyzes its historical emergence under specific French class conditions while Bakunin treats all state existence as inherently incompatible with freedom.

1. **Marx's View in Poverty of Philosophy**:
   - Marx critiques P.J. Proudhon's economic and philosophical doctrine, particularly Proudhon's application of the Ricardian theory that the entire social product belongs to the workers as their product because they are the sole real producers.

   - Mill advocates for free trade, stating that leaving producers and sellers perfectly free, under the sole check of equal freedom to the buyers, is the most effective way to ensure cheapness and good quality of commodities.

Karl Marx's conclusion in "Value, Price and Profit" regarding wage struggles contrasts with Mikhail Bakunin's characterization of capital in "The Capitalist System" in several ways:

1. **Wage Struggles and Capitalism**:
   - **Marx** argues that wage struggles are a natural and necessary part of the capitalist system. He states that the struggle to raise wages is a reaction to the fluctuations in the market, such as changes in the value of labor, the value of money, and the intensity of labor. Marx sees these struggles as inevitable and part of the ongoing conflict between capital and labor.
   - **Bakunin** views the capitalist system as inherently exploitative and sees the wage relationship as a form of slavery. He argues that the growth of the population outstrips the growth of production, leading to a relative sinking of the level of wages. He sees the capitalist system as a mechanism that continually pushes workers into a state of serfdom, with the threat of starvation always looming.

2. **Nature of Freedom**:
   - **Marx** acknowledges that workers have the theoretical freedom to quit their employers, but he points out that this freedom is often illusory due to the economic constraints workers face. He argues that workers are driven to continue working due to the necessity of earning a living.
   - **Bakunin** is more critical, describing the worker's freedom as "fictitious" and "utter falsehood" because the economic conditions force workers to continue working under exploitative conditions.

3. **Economic Exploitation**:
   - **Marx** explains that the struggle between capital and labor is a result of the capitalist system's inherent contradictions, such as the periodic resistance of workers against wage reductions and the attempts to raise wages. He sees the struggle as a means for workers to assert their value and challenge the exploitation by capital.
   - **Bakunin** sees the capitalist system as a mechanism that exploits the labor of the proletariat, pushing them into a state of perpetual competition and exploitation. He describes the capitalist system as one where the growth of the population outstrips the growth of production, leading to a relative sinking of wages and the proletarianization of the petty bourgeoisie.

In summary, while both Marx and Bakunin critique the capitalist system, they do so from different perspectives. Marx sees the struggle as a necessary part of the capitalist system, while Bakunin views the system as inherently exploitative and sees the wage relationship as a form of slavery.
reference: In Value, Price and Profit, Marx argues that workers must go beyond daily wage resistance and demand the 'Abolition of the wages system!' because capitalism engenders the material conditions needed to reconstruct society. In The Capitalist System, Bakunin describes capital and property as a state-guaranteed right to live without working by exploiting those who own no property and are forced by hunger to sell their labor power. Both authors agree that capitalist property relations inherently rely on compulsory labor exploitation, with Marx urging the working class to replace the wage system entirely and Bakunin emphasizing that capital is fundamentally state-sanctioned non-productive exploitation.

Based on the provided context, Marx and Bakunin have different focuses and approaches to the issue of alienated labor and wage labor, but both critique the capitalist system.

Marx's analysis, as presented in the context, centers on the alienation of labor within the capitalist mode of production. He argues that under capitalism, labor is alienated from the worker, the product, and the species-being (human potential). Specifically, Marx sees the capitalist system as creating a contradiction where labor is the sole source of exchange-value and use-value, yet it is treated as a mere cost and instrument of production. This leads to the exploitation of workers, who are reduced to wage-labor and face the alienation of their own productive power.

Bakunin, on the other hand, focuses more on the broader social and political implications of wage labor. He critiques the state and the capitalist system as a whole, seeing the state as a class in itself that perpetuates inequality. Bakunin argues that the state and the political structures it supports are not just an agent of the dominant economic class but also a class in itself, exercising a monopoly of armed force and sovereignty. He sees the state as a mechanism that traps workers in poverty and perpetuates social and economic inequality.

While Marx's analysis is more focused on the economic and social relations within the capitalist system, Bakunin's critique is broader, encompassing the political and social structures that enable and perpetuate the conditions of wage labor and poverty. Marx does not explicitly discuss how wage labor traps workers in poverty in the provided context, but his analysis of alienated labor suggests that the conditions of wage labor under capitalism lead to exploitation and the alienation of workers from their labor and its products.

In summary, Marx's analysis of alienated labor is more about the internal contradictions and exploitation within the capitalist system, while Bakunin's critique is more about the broader social and political structures that enable and perpetuate the conditions of wage labor and poverty.
reference: In the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx explains the philosophical mechanics of alienation, noting that as the world of things gains value, the worker is devalued and converted into a commodity whose product confronts him as an alien power. In The Capitalist System, Bakunin describes the practical economic trap of wage labor, showing how the worker's poverty forces him to sell his labor at the lowest price, which continuously reproduces and deepens his poverty. While Marx focuses on how labor's product becomes an independent alien force dominating the worker, Bakunin emphasizes the self-perpetuating cycle of poverty and price depression that keeps wage laborers economically trapped.

And that this one will feel, let us say, a greater liberty and, in practical terms, show a greater aptitude and capability than his fellow? It is natural that he who knows more will dominate him who knows less. And were this disparity of education and education and learning the only one to exist between two classes, would not all the others swiftly follow until the world of men itself in its present circumstances, that is, until it was again divided into a mass of slaves and a tiny number of rulers, the former labouring away as they do today, to the advantage of the latter?', 'That example gives a roughly accurate notion of the respective advances made by the bourgeoisie and the proletariat. To sum up. In society as presently constituted, the advances of science have been at the root of the relative ignorance of the proletariat, just as the progress of industry and commerce have been at the root of its relative impoverishment. Thus, intellectual progress and material progress have contributed in equal measure towards the exacerbation of the slavery of the proletariat. Meaning what? Meaning that we have a duty to reject and resist that bourgeois science, just as we have a duty to reject and resist bourgeois wealth. L’Égalité

According to John Stuart Mill's description in "Auguste Comte and Positivism," Auguste Comte views political expertise as something that should be based on scientific knowledge and the application of positivism. Mill notes that Comte believes in the sovereignty of the people and that after proper education, individuals should be allowed to find their places in society, which would naturally lead to a classification that aligns with their aptitudes.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin in "Equal Opportunity in Education" criticizes the current state of science and education, which he sees as benefiting only the privileged classes. Bakunin argues that the advances in science and industry have contributed to the exploitation and relative impoverishment of the proletariat. He advocates for an equal education for all, rejecting the idea that science and education should be the preserve of a privileged few.

response:
John Stuart Mill and Mikhail Bakunin both critique the tyranny of majority opinion, but they do so from different perspectives and with different emphases.

Bakunin describes social tyranny as a pervasive influence that operates through customs, mores, and habits, which collectively form public opinion. He argues that this social tyranny is more insidious and powerful than the formal authority of the state because it is more pervasive and insidious, affecting individuals from birth and shaping their very identities. Bakunin sees the revolt against social tyranny as more difficult because it requires individuals to confront and overcome the deeply ingrained influences of society.

Mill, on the other hand, focuses on the tyranny of the majority as a form of social oppression that can be exercised through collective opinion and feeling, not just through the actions of public authorities. He warns that society can impose its will on individuals through social pressure and norms, even without legal penalties. Mill emphasizes the need for protection against this tyranny of the majority, advocating for the freedom of individuals to dissent from prevailing opinions and to develop their own character.

While both authors recognize the dangers of majority tyranny, Bakunin's focus is more on the natural and insidious influence of society, while Mill's concerns are more about the collective opinion and feeling of society as a whole. Bakunin sees the state as a transitory institution that can be revolted against, whereas Mill's critique is more about the ongoing influence of society on individuals.
reference: Both Mill in On Liberty and Bakunin in Man, Society, and Freedom observe that non-legal, social pressure can be just as formidable as formal political despotism. Mill stresses that social tyranny penetrates deeply into daily life to enslave the soul and stifle individuality through prevailing feelings and opinion without needing civil penalties. Bakunin similarly describes social tyranny as gentle, insidious, and unformalized, operating through customs, prejudices, and public opinion rather than state laws or judicial punishment. Both thinkers highlight that public opinion and societal expectations exert an all-pervasive, coercive force on human behavior independent of state legislation.

John Stuart Mill's doctrine in "Principles of Political Economy" and Karl Marx's critique in "Capital, Volume 1" present contrasting views on the relationship between capital, production, and the demand for labor. Here are some key points of comparison:

### John Stuart Mill's View

1. **Capital as a Requisite for Production**: Mill emphasizes that capital is a necessary condition for production. He argues that capital enables the accumulation of means of production, which in turn allows for more extensive and efficient labor.

2. **Demand for Labor and Capital**: Mill posits that an increase in capital leads to an increase in the demand for labor, as more capital can support more labor. He believes that the demand for labor is not directly related to the amount of capital but rather to the productivity of labor.

3. **Productive and Unproductive Labor**: Mill distinguishes between productive and unproductive labor, arguing that productive labor contributes to the production of wealth, while unproductive labor does not. He suggests that the demand for productive labor is more stable and beneficial.

4. **Capital as a Source of Employment**: Mill argues that capital can create more employment opportunities, as it allows for the expansion of production and the creation of new industries. He sees capital as a means to increase the overall wealth and employment in society.

### Karl Marx's Critique

1. **Critique of Compensation Theories**: Marx critiques the idea that the capitalist system can adequately compensate workers for their labor. He argues that the capitalist mode of production inherently exploits workers by appropriating the surplus value produced by their labor.

2. **Surplus Value and Exploitation**: Marx introduces the concept of surplus value, which is the difference between the value of labor power and the value of the commodities produced by labor. He argues that capitalists appropriate this surplus value, leading to the exploitation of workers.

3. **Labor as a Commodity**: Marx views labor as a commodity that is bought and sold in the market. However, he argues that the value of labor power is determined by the minimum subsistence requirements of the worker, not by the value of the commodities produced.

4. **Capital as a Social Relation**: Marx sees capital not just as a means of production but as a social relation of exploitation. He argues that the capitalist system is characterized by the alienation of workers from their labor and the means of production.

5. **Critique of the Demand for Labor**: Marx does not see the demand for labor as a positive outcome of capital accumulation. Instead, he argues that the demand for labor is driven by the need to extract surplus value, which is a result of the capitalist mode of production.

### Key Differences

- **Purpose of Capital**: Mill sees capital as a means to increase production and employment, while Marx views it as a tool of exploitation.
- **Nature of Labor**: Mill sees labor as productive and valuable, while Marx sees it as a source of exploitation.
- **Outcome of Capital Accumulation**: Mill believes that capital accumulation leads to increased demand for labor, while Marx argues that it leads to the exploitation of labor.

In summary, while Mill sees capital as a positive force that increases the demand for labor and contributes to overall wealth, Marx views it as a mechanism of exploitation that inherently leads to the oppression of workers.
reference: In Principles of Political Economy, Mill argues that demand for commodities is not a demand for labor, asserting that only capital directly advanced in wages supports and employs laborers. In Capital, Volume 1, Marx explicitly attacks Mill and other economists for claiming that introducing machinery automatically 'sets free' capital to re-employ displaced workers. Marx satirizes this economic dogma, contending that machinery actually deprives workers of their means of subsistence rather than liberating capital for their benefit. While Mill sees capital as the sole protective mechanism for labor employment, Marx argues that capital transformation under mechanization actively locks up variable capital and displaces workers.

Whosoever mentions the State, implies force, oppression, exploitation, injustice-all these brought together as a system are the main condition of present-day society. The State has never had, and never can have, a morality. Its only morality and justice is its own interest, its existence, and its omnipotence at any price; and before its interest, all interest of humanity must stand in the back-ground. The State is the negation of Humanity. It is this in two ways: the opposite of human freedom and human justice (internally), as well as the forcible disruption of the common solidarity of mankind (externally).The Universal State, repeatedly attempted, has always proved an impossibility, so that as long as the State exists, States will exist and since every State regards itself as absolute, and proclaims the adoration of its power as the highest law, to which all other laws must be subordinated, it therefore follows that as long as States exist wars cannot cease. Every State must conquer, or be conquered. Every State must build its power on the weakness or, if it can do it without danger to itself, on the destruction, of other States.', 'To strive for international justice, liberty, and perpetual peace, and at the same time to uphold the State, is contradictory and naive. It is impossible to alter the nature of the State, because it is just this nature that constitutes the State; and States cannot change their nature without ceasing to exist. It thus follows that there cannot be a good, just, virtuous State. All States are bad in that sense, that they, by their nature, by their principle, by their very foundation and the highest ideal of their existence, are the opponents of human liberty, morality, and justice. And in this regard there is, one may say what one likes, no great difference between the barbaric Russian Empire and the civilized States of Europe. Wherein lies the only difference ? Russian Tsardom does openly what the others do under the mask of hypocrisy. Tsardom, with its undisguised political method, and its contempt for humanity, is the only goal to which all statesmen of Europe secretly but envyingly aspire. All States of Europe do the same as Russia, as far as public opinion, and especially as far as the reawakened but very powerful solidarity of the people allow them-a public opinion and solidarity which contain in themselves the gems of the destruction of States. There is no “good” State, with the possible exception of those that are powerless. And even they are quite criminal enough in their dreams. He who wants freedom, justice, and peace, he who wants the entire (economic and political) liberation of the masses, must strive for the destruction of the States, and the establishment of a universal federation of free groups for Production.', 'As long as the German workers strive for the establishment of a national State-however popular and free they may imagine this State (and there is a far stop from imagination to realization, especially when there is the fraternization of two diametrically opposed principles, the State and the liberty of the people, involved)-so long will they Sacrifice the liberty of the people to the might of the State, Socialism to politics, international justice and fraternity to patriotism. It is clear that their own economic liberation will remain a beautiful dream, looming in the distant future.

It is impossible to reach two opposite poles simultaneously. Socialism, the Social Revolution, presupposes the abolition of the State; it is therefore clear that he who is in favor of the State must give up Socialism, and sacrifice the economic liberation of the workers to the political power of some privileged party.

The German Social Democratic Party is forced to sacrifice the economic liberation of the proletariat, and consequently also their political liberation- or, better expressed, their liberation from politics-to the self-seeking and triumph of the bourgeois Democracy. This follows unquestionably from Articles 2 and 3 of their program. The first three paragraphs of Article 2 are quite in accord with the Socialist principles of the International, whose programming they copy nearly literally. But the fourth paragraph of the same article, which declares that political liberty is the forerunner of economic liberty, entirely destroys the practical value of the recognition of our principles. It can mean nothing else than this:- —', '“Proletarians, you are slaves, the victims of private property and capitalism. You want to liberate yourselves from this yoke. This is good, and your demands are quite just. But in order to realize them, you must help us to accomplish the political revolution. Afterwards we will help you to accomplish the Social Revolution. Let us therefore, through the might of your arms establish the Democratic State, and then-and then we will create commonweal for you, similar to the one the Swiss workers enjoy.”

In order to convince oneself that this preposterous delusion expresses entirely the spirit and tendency of the German Social Democratic Party-i.e.,their program, not the natural aspirations of the German workers, of whom the party consists-one need only study the third article of this program, wherein all the initial demands, which shall be brought about by the peaceful and legal agitation of the party, are elaborated. All these demands, with the exception of the tenth, which had not even been proposed by the authors of the program, but had been added later-during the discussion, by a member of the Eisenach Congress-all these demands are of an entirely political character. All those points which are recommended as the main object of the immediate practical activity of the party consist of nothing else but the well known program of bourgeois Democracy; universal suffrage, with direct legislation by the people, abolition of all political privilege; a citizen army; separation of Church and State, and school and State; free and compulsory education; liberty of the Press assembly, and combination; conversion of all indirect taxation into a direct, progressive, and universal income-tax.', 'Produced by Curtis A. CONSIDERATIONS ON REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNMENT

By John Stuart Mill


Author Of "A System Of Logic, Ratiocinative And Inductive"

Preface


Those who have done me the honor of reading my previous writings will
probably receive no strong impression of novelty from the present
volume; for the principles are those to which I have been working up
during the greater part of my life, and most of the practical
suggestions have been anticipated by others or by myself. There is
novelty, however, in the fact of bringing them together, and
exhibiting them in their connection, and also, I believe, in much that
is brought forward in their support. Several of the opinions at all
events, if not new, are for the present as little likely to meet with
general acceptance as if they were.', 'The present is one of the many instances in which, as I have already
had occasion to remark, the _spirit_ of an institution, the impression
it makes on the mind of the citizen, is one of the most important
parts of its operation. The spirit of vote by ballot--the
interpretation likely to be put on it in the mind of an elector, is
that the suffrage is given to him for himself--for his particular use
and benefit, and not as a trust for the public. For if it is indeed a
trust, if the public are entitled to his vote, are not they entitled
to know his vote? This false and pernicious impression may well be
made on the generality, since it has been made on most of those who of
late years have been conspicuous advocates of the ballot. The doctrine
was not so understood by its earlier promoters; but the effect of a
doctrine on the mind is best shown, not in those who form it, but in
those who are formed by it. Mr. Bright and his school of democrats
think themselves greatly concerned in maintaining that the franchise
is what they term a right, not a trust. Now this one idea, taking root
in the general mind, does a moral mischief outweighing all the good
that the ballot could do, at the highest possible estimate of it. In
whatever way we define or understand the idea of a right, no person
can have a right (except in the purely legal sense) to power over
others: every such power, which he is allowed to possess is morally,
in the fullest force of the term, a trust. But the exercise of any
political function, either as an elector or as a representative, is
power over others. Those who say that the suffrage is not a trust, but
a right, will scarcely accept the conclusions to which their doctrine', 'In any political election, even by universal suffrage (and still more
obviously in the case of a restricted suffrage), the voter is under an
absolute moral obligation to consider the interest of the public, not
his private advantage, and give his vote, to the best of his judgment,
exactly as he would be bound to do if he were the sole voter, and the
election depended upon him alone. This being admitted, it is at least
a _prima facie_ consequence that the duty of voting, like any other
public duty, should be performed under the eye and criticism of the
public; every one of whom has not only an interest in its performance,
but a good title to consider himself wronged if it is performed
otherwise than honestly and carefully. Undoubtedly neither this nor
any other maxim of political morality is absolutely inviolable; it may
be overruled by still more cogent considerations. But its weight is
such that the cases which admit of a departure from it must be of a
strikingly exceptional character.', 'It seems to me, however, from various indications, and from none more
than the recent debates on Reform of Parliament, that both
Conservatives and Liberals (if I may continue to call them what they
still call themselves) have lost confidence in the political creeds
which they nominally profess, while neither side appears to have made
any progress in providing itself with a better. Yet such a better
doctrine must be possible; not a mere compromise, by splitting the
difference between the two, but something wider than either, which, in
virtue of its superior comprehensiveness, might be adopted by either
Liberal or Conservative without renouncing any thing which he really
feels to be valuable in his own creed. When so many feel obscurely the
want of such a doctrine, and so few even flatter themselves that they
have attained it, any one may without presumption, offer what his own
thoughts, and the best that he knows of those of others, are able to
contribute towards its formation.

response:
Bakunin and Mill have fundamentally different views on the nature of the state and its relationship to individual freedom and justice.

Bakunin views the state as inherently immoral and oppressive. He argues that the state's only morality is its own existence and power, and that it is the negation of human freedom and justice. For Bakunin, the state is an institution that must be destroyed to achieve true freedom, justice, and peace. He sees no possibility of reforming the state to make it just or virtuous, as he believes its nature is fundamentally opposed to human liberty and morality.

In contrast, Mill's perspective on the state is more pragmatic. He acknowledges that the state can be a necessary institution, but he emphasizes the importance of the spirit and moral character of the state and its institutions. Mill believes that the state should serve the public good and that the suffrage should be seen as a trust for the public, not just a personal right. He argues that voters have a moral obligation to consider the public interest when voting, and that the state should be accountable to the public. Mill does not advocate for the complete abolition of the state but rather for a form of representative government that can be reformed and improved.

Thus, while Bakunin sees the state as an irredeemable evil, Mill sees it as a potentially beneficial institution that can be made more just and accountable through proper governance and the active participation of citizens.
reference: In The German Crisis, Bakunin characterizes the state as an inherently immoral system of force, oppression, and exploitation whose sole interest is its own omnipotence at the expense of humanity. In contrast, Mill asserts in Considerations on Representative Government that political voting within a representative state carries an absolute moral obligation to serve the public interest rather than personal advantage. While Mill believes state electoral mechanisms can express civic duty and public morality, Bakunin maintains that the state is fundamentally devoid of morality and exists only to subjugate human freedom.

Karl Marx's critique of bourgeois capital categories in Capital, Volume 2, and John Stuart Mill's formulation of wage determination in Principles of Political Economy, present contrasting perspectives on the nature of capital and the dynamics of labor and wages. Here are the key differences:

### Marx's Critique in Capital, Volume 2

1. **Nature of Capital**:
   - **Constant and Variable Capital**: Marx distinguishes between constant capital (capital invested in means of production) and variable capital (capital invested in labor-power). He argues that the distinction between fixed and circulating capital is not as significant as the distinction between constant and variable capital.
   - **Durability and Perishability**: Marx notes that all capital is perishable, with varying degrees of durability. This obliterates the specific differences between capital invested in labor-power and capital invested in means of production.

2. **Critique of Ricardo**:
   - Marx criticizes David Ricardo's theory of value and profit, which he sees as a theory of surplus-value. Marx argues that Ricardo's classification of fixed and circulating capital is flawed and does not properly distinguish between constant and variable capital.
   - Marx contends that the definitions of fixed and circulating capital are misleading and obscure the specific nature of variable capital, which is the capital invested in labor-power.

3. **Labor and Capital**:
   - Marx emphasizes the importance of labor in the production process, viewing labor as the source of surplus-value. He argues that the distinction between fixed and circulating capital is not as significant as the distinction between constant and variable capital, which is central to understanding the exploitation of labor.

### Mill's Formulation in Principles of Political Economy

1. **Wage Fund Theory**:
   - **Wage Fund**: Mill introduces the concept of a "wage fund," which is the total amount of capital set aside for the payment of wages. He argues that the size of this fund determines the level of wages.
   - **Economic Law**: Mill posits that there is a predetermined amount of wealth that will be paid in wages, and this amount is determined by the total capital available in the economy.

2. **Capital and Labor**:
   - **Capital Accumulation**: Mill discusses the process of capital accumulation and how it influences the distribution of wages. He argues that the desire for accumulation and the size of the capital fund are key determinants of wages.
   - **Labor's Role**: Mill acknowledges the role of labor in the production process but places more emphasis on the capital fund as the primary determinant of wages.

3. **Critique of Overproduction**:
   - Mill addresses the issue of overproduction, which was a concern among some economists of his time. He argues that the amount of capital available for wages is predetermined and that the labor market is regulated by this fund.

### Key Differences

1. **Nature of Capital**:
   - **Marx**: Focuses on the distinction between constant and variable capital, emphasizing the role of labor in the production process.
   - **Mill**: Emphasizes the wage fund and the total capital available, viewing labor as a factor in the distribution of wages.

2. **Labor and Exploitation**:
   - **Marx**: Sees labor as the source of surplus-value and the exploitation of labor as central to the capitalist system.
   - **Mill**: Views labor as a factor in the production process but places more emphasis on the capital fund as the primary determinant of wages.

3. **Economic Determinism**:
   - **Marx**: Argues that the capitalist system is inherently exploitative and that the labor process is central to the production of surplus-value.
   - **Mill**: Sees the economy as a system where the distribution of wages is determined by the total capital available, but still acknowledges the role of labor in the production process.

In summary, Marx's critique in Capital, Volume 2 focuses on the exploitation of labor and the nature of capital, while Mill's formulation in Principles of Political Economy emphasizes the wage fund and the role of capital in determining wages.

In Principles of Political Economy (as excerpted via Cairnes's restatement), Mill treats capital and wages through investment proportions, holding that profit expectations and investment forms determine the predetermined share of capital paid out as wages to laborers. While Mill analyzes wage-fund allocation based on circulation and investment proportions, Marx insists that such circulation-focused frameworks obscure the fundamental distinction between value-creating variable capital and constant capital.

Marx criticizes the demand for compound interest as unsustainable, as it cannot be met by the productive powers of labor alone.

Marx does not explicitly describe the labor market in the same terms as Bakunin, but he does highlight the exploitative nature of capital accumulation and the resulting crises.

Both authors highlight the exploitative nature of the capitalist system, but they focus on different aspects of it.

   - **Mill**: According to Mill, rent is the excess of the return from agricultural land over the return from the worst land in cultivation. He attributes rent to the difference in productivity between different pieces of land, stating that the rent is the surplus produced by more fertile land beyond what the least productive land can produce.
   - **Marx**: Marx, on the other hand, views rent as a form of surplus value that arises from the capitalist mode of production. He argues that rent is not simply a result of the natural productivity of the land but is a product of the capitalist relations of production. Specifically, Marx contends that rent is a form of surplus value paid by agricultural capital to landowners after the equalization of surplus value to the average profit among various capitals.

2. **Role of Capitalism**:
   - **Mill**: Mill's analysis does not explicitly emphasize the role of capitalism in the formation of rent. He focuses more on the natural differences in land productivity and the resulting economic outcomes.
   - **Marx**: Marx's analysis is deeply rooted in the capitalist mode of production. He sees rent as a consequence of the class struggle and the unequal distribution of surplus value among different classes (landowners, capitalists, and wage-laborers).

3. **Distribution of Surplus Value**:
   - **Mill**: Mill's theory does not delve into the distribution of surplus value among different classes. He primarily discusses the economic conditions under which rent arises.
   - **Marx**: Marx's analysis includes a detailed examination of how surplus value is distributed among different classes in capitalist society, with rent being a specific form of this distribution.

4. **Historical Context and Practical Motives**:
   - **Marx**: Marx's work includes a critique of earlier economists and their attempts to explain rent. He notes that many earlier economists failed to understand the true source of rent within the capitalist system.
   - **Mill**: Mill's focus is more on the economic principles and laws governing rent, without a detailed critique of previous economic theories.

Mikhail Bakunin's principle of voluntary federation in "Principles and Organization of the International Revolutionary Society" and John Stuart Mill's view of public spirit in "Considerations on Representative Government" share some commonalities but also have significant differences.

### Commonalities:

1. **Voluntary Association and Participation:**
   - **Bakunin:** Emphasizes the importance of voluntary associations and groups based on shared interests. He believes that individuals should unite according to their real interests, creating a unity of purpose and well-being.
   - **Mill:** Advocates for the importance of individual participation and the spirit of public engagement. He argues that the suffrage should be seen as a trust for the public, not just a personal right.

2. **Critique of Hierarchical Structures:**
   - **Bakunin:** Sees the State as an artificial and oppressive institution that limits human fellowship and equality. He opposes the State because it uses the power of the masses to enforce its rule in an authoritarian manner.
   - **Mill:** Critiques bureaucratic and hierarchical structures, noting that they can stifle individual energy and lead to routine and stagnation. He advocates for a popular government that can harness the creativity and initiative of individuals.

### Differences:

1. **Nature of the State and Society:**
   - **Bakunin:** Views the State as inherently oppressive and a negation of human society. He advocates for a voluntary federation of workers' associations that operate outside the State framework.
   - **Mill:** While critical of the State, he does not entirely reject it. He advocates for a representative democracy where the people have a say in governance, but he also recognizes the potential for abuse of power and the need for checks and balances.

2. **Role of the Individual:**
   - **Bakunin:** Emphasizes the individual's role in voluntary associations and the collective action of the working class. He sees the individual as a member of a larger, self-organizing society.
   - **Mill:** Focuses on the individual's role in public life and the importance of public spirit. He argues that the individual should participate in public functions and that the suffrage should be seen as a responsibility to the community.

3. **Means of Achieving Social Change:**
   - **Bakunin:** Sees the International as a means to unite workers and create a new, equitable society through voluntary association and collective action.
   - **Mill:** Sees representative government as a means to achieve social change through the participation of the people in the political process. He advocates for a system where the people can influence and shape the government through their representatives.

4. **View of Power and Influence:**
   - **Bakunin:** Sees power as something to be shared and distributed among the people through voluntary associations, rather than concentrated in a hierarchical state.
   - **Mill:** Sees power as something that should be exercised responsibly and with the consent of the governed, but acknowledges that it can be abused if not properly checked.

In summary, while both Bakunin and Mill advocate for a more participatory and democratic form of governance, Bakunin's vision is more radical and focuses on the abolition of the State and the creation of a voluntary federation, whereas Mill's view is more moderate and seeks to reform existing representative institutions to better serve the public interest.

Both thinkers highlight local self-governance and voluntary association as essential for genuine social cohesion, though Bakunin frames it as an absolute revolutionary right against the state, whereas Mill views local participation as a moral and educational mechanism within representative government.
