Whatever the fairness or accuracy of such a depiction – and it should be kept in mind that Marx, Lassalle, and the new German Social-Democratic Party, all of whom Bakunin lumps together, actually held different views on many issues – it is the product of a degree of literary skill for which Bakunin is rarely given credit.', 'In opposition to both statism and Marxism, Bakunin presents in broad outline the principles of “anarchy,” as he calls what we would today term anarchism, and the anarchist society of the future. In the most general terms it can be said that each of the three competing political ideologies of the nineteenth century, liberalism, socialism, and anarchism, took its stand primarily on one element of the French Revolution’s trinity, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity. Anarchism joined socialism in rejecting nineteenth-century parliamentarism, or “bourgeois democracy,” as a narrow conception of liberty which could be enjoyed only by the propertied classes as long as economic inequality prevailed. The anarchist critique of liberalism added little to that of the socialists, and the pages of
Statism and Anarchy
dealing with this subject are perhaps the least original – and, in retrospect, some of the most short-sighted – in the book. Much more original was anarchism’s critique of Marxism as inherently unable to achieve the true economic equality it claimed to represent. Bakunin was the first to warn that Marxists in power might simply replace the capitalists they had chased out, leaving the position of the workers essentially unchanged, and after him it became a major component of anarchist thought.', 'Equally repellent, though less marked in this work than in some others, is Bakunin’s anti-Semitism, which often appeared as a corollary to his anti-Germanism. It may be argued that such sentiments, however distasteful, do not negate Bakunin’s anarchist principles.[29] It may also be argued that those principles are somehow deficient if even one so passionately committed to them was unable to surmount crude ethnic prejudices. John Stuart Mill's argument for gender equality in "The Subjection of Women" and Marx and Engels' critique of bourgeois marriage in the Manifesto of the Communist Party share some common themes but also have distinct differences.

Both authors critique the existing social structures that limit women's freedom and autonomy. Mill argues that the principle of legal subordination of women to men is wrong and hinders human improvement. He advocates for a principle of perfect equality between the sexes, rejecting any power or privilege on one side and any disability on the other.

Marx and Engels, in their critique of bourgeois marriage, also highlight the subordination of women. They state that bourgeois marriage is a system of wives in common, where women are seen merely as instruments of production. They argue that the intervention of society in education should be altered to rescue it from the influence of the ruling class, which includes the bourgeois view of marriage.

However, there are key differences:
- Mill focuses more on the individual rights and personal enjoyment of women, arguing that restrictions on women's freedom reduce human happiness and hinder social progress.
- Marx and Engels focus on the broader social and economic context, linking the subordination of women to the class struggle and the capitalist system. They see the subordination of women as part of a larger system of exploitation and oppression.

In summary, while both authors critique the existing social structures that limit women's freedom, Mill emphasizes individual rights and personal happiness, whereas Marx and Engels emphasize the broader social and economic context of class struggle and capitalist exploitation.

['th
, 2009 from [[http://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/bakunin/works/1871/paris-commune.htm][www.marxists.org]]
#notes Source: Bakunin on Anarchy, translated and edited by Sam Dolgoff, 1971



This work, like all my published work, of which there has not been a great deal, is an outgrowth of events. It is the natural continuation of my
Letters to a Frenchman
(September 1870), wherein I had the easy but painful distinction of foreseeing and foretelling the dire calamities which now beset France and the whole civilized world, the only cure for which is the Social Revolution.

My purpose now is to prove the need for such a revolution. I shall review the historical development of society and what is now taking place in Europe, right before our eyes. Thus all those who sincerely thirst for truth can accept it and proclaim openly and unequivocally the philosophical principles and practical aims which are at the very core of what we call the Social Revolution.

I know my self-imposed task is not a simple one. I might be called presumptuous had I any personal motives in undertaking it. Let me assure my reader, I have none. I am not a scholar or a philosopher, not even a professional writer. I have not done much writing in my life and have never written except, so to speak, in self-defense, and only when a passionate conviction forced me to overcome my instinctive dislike for any public exhibition of myself.', 'This was a great misfortune for the Commune and for these men. They were paralyzed, and they paralyzed the Commune. Yet we cannot blame them. Men are not transformed overnight; they do not change their natures or their habits at will. They proved their sincerity by letting themselves be killed for the Commune. Who would dare ask more of them?

They are no more to be blamed than the people of Paris, under whose influence they thought and acted. The people were socialists more by instinct than by reflection. All their aspirations are in the highest degree socialist but their ideas, or rather their traditional expressions, are not. The proletariat of the great cities of France, and even of Paris, still cling to many Jacobin prejudices, and to many dictatorial and governmental concepts. The cult of authority — the fatal result of religious education, that historic source of all evils, deprivations, and servitude — has not yet been completely eradicated in them. This is so true that even the most intelligent children of the people, the most convinced socialists, have not freed themselves completely of these ideas. If you rummage around a bit in their minds, you will find the Jacobin, the advocate of government, cowering in a dark corner, humble but not quite dead.', 'I know that many socialists, very logical in their theory, blame our Paris friends for not having acted sufficiently as socialists in their revolutionary practice. The yelping pack of the bourgeois press, on the other hand, accuse them of having followed their program too faithfully. Let us forget, for a moment, the ignoble denunciations of that press. I want to call the attention of the strictest theoreticians of proletarian emancipation to the fact that they are unjust to our Paris brothers, for between the most correct theories and their practical application lies an enormous distance which cannot be bridged in a few days. Whoever had the pleasure of knowing Varlin, for instance (to name just one man whose death is certain), knows that he and his friends were guided by profound, passionate, and well-considered socialist convictions. These were men whose ardent zeal, devotion, and good faith had never been questioned by those who had known them. Yet, precisely because they were men of good faith, they were filled with self-distrust in the face of the immense task to which they had devoted their minds and their lives; they thought too little of themselves! And they were convinced that in the Social Revolution, diametrically opposite to a political revolution in this as in other ways, individual action was to be almost nil, while the spontaneous action of the masses had to be everything. All that individuals can do is formulate, clarify, and propagate ideas expressing the instinctive desires of the people, and contribute their constant efforts to the revolutionary organization of the natural powers of the masses. This and nothing more; all the rest can be accomplished only by the people themselves. Otherwise we would end up with a political dictatorship — the reconstitution of the State, with all its privileges, inequalities, and oppressions; by taking a devious but inevitable path we would come to reestablish the political, social, and economic slavery of the masses.', 'Our Paris friends were right a thousand times over. In fact, where is the mind, brilliant as it may be, or — if we speak of a collective dictatorship, even if it were formed of several hundred individuals endowed with superior mentalities — where are the intellects powerful enough to embrace the infinite multiplicity and diversity of real interests, aspirations, wishes, and needs which sum up the collective will of the people? And to invent a social organization that will not be a Procrustean bed upon which the violence of the State will more or less overtly force unhappy society to stretch out? It has always been thus, and it is exactly this old system of organization by force that the Social Revolution should end by granting full liberty to the masses, the groups, the communes, the associations and to the individuals as well; by destroying once and for all the historic cause of all violence, which is the power and indeed the mere existence of the State. Its fall will bring down with it all the inequities of the law and all the lies of the various religions, since both law and religion have never been anything but the compulsory consecration, ideal and real, of all violence represented, guaranteed, and protected by the State.', 'The principal defect of the moral systems taught in the past was to have been either exclusively socialist or exclusively individualist. Thus the civic morality, as it has been transmitted to us by the Greeks and Romans, was an exclusively socialist morality, in the sense that it always sacrificed individuality to the collectivity. Without speaking of the myriads of slaves, which would constitute the whole basis of ancient civilization, not even counting them only as things, the individuality [of the] Greek or Roman citizen himself was always patriotically immolated for the profit of the collectivity established as a State. And when the citizens, tired of this permanent sacrifice, no longer wanted to allow it and would refuse the sacrifice, the republics, first Greek, then Roman, would collapse. The awakening of individualism caused the death of antiquity.

It finds its purest and most complete expression in the monotheistic religions, in Judaism, in Mohammedanism and in Christianity especially. The Jehovah of the Jews still addresses himself to the collectivity, at least in certain regards, since he has a chosen people, although he already contains all the seeds of the exclusively individualist morality.

It had to be so: the gods of Greek and Roman antiquity were in the last analysis only symbols, the supreme representatives of the deified collectivity, of the State. by worshipping them, they worshipped the State, and all the morals that were taught in their name could consequently have no other object than the safety, grandeur and glory of the State.', 'Under this unhealthy influence, the mind is obscured and the ardent search for truth is transformed into a complaisant worship of lies; human dignity is debased, honesty becomes treacherous, kindness cruel, justice iniquitous and human respect is transformed into an arrogant disdain for men; the instinct for liberty leads to the establishment of servitude, and Charity, becoming informer and persecutor, ordered the massacre of the heretics and the bloody orgies of the inquisition—the religious man was called Jesuit, momier or pietist—renouncing humanity, he aims for sanctity—and the saint under the guise of a more or less hypocritical humility and charity, conceal the pride and immense selfishness of an absolutely isolated human ego, which worships itself in its God. For we must not be mistaken, what the religious man seeks above all and thinks that he finds in the Divinity that he worships, is still himself, but glorified, invested with infinite power and immortalized. And he has too often drawn from it pretexts and instruments to enslave and exploit the human world.

That then is the last word of the Christian cult; it is the exaltation selfishness, which, breaking all social solidarity, worships itself in its God and imposes itself on the ignorant mass of men in the name of that God, which is to say in the name of its human Self, consciously or unconsciously exalted and deified by itself. That is also why religious men are ordinarily so fierce: in defending their God, they take part for their selfishness, their pride, and their vanity.

From all this it results that Christianity is the most decisive and more complete negation of all solidarity between men, that is of society, and consequently also of morals, since outside of society, there can be no morality, there remains only the religious relations of the isolated man with his God, which is to say with himself.', 'Man, as an individual animal, like the animals of all the other species, at first glance and as soon as he begins to breathe, has the immediate sentiment of his individual existence; but he acquires reflective consciousness of himself, conscience which properly constitutes his personality, by means of intelligence, and consequently only in society. Your innermost personality, the consciousness that you have of yourself in your heart of hearts, is at it were only the reflection of your own image, echoed and sent back to you as if by so many mirrors, by the consciousness, both collective and individual, of all the human beings that make up your social world. Each man that you know and with whom you have found yourself in relations, whether direct of indirect, determines, more or less, your most intimate being, contributes to making you what you are, to forming your personality.

Consequently, if you are surrounded by slaves, though you are their master, you are no less a slave, the consciousness of the slaves only being able to reflect back your image in degraded form. The stupidity of everyone makes you stupid, while the intelligence of all enlightens you, raises you up; the vices of your social milieu are your vices, and you do not know how to be a really free man, if you are not surrounded by equally free men, the existence of a single slave is sufficient to diminish your liberty. In the immortal declaration of the rights of man, made by the National Convention we find clearly expressed that sublime truth that “
the slavery of one single human being is the slavery of all
.”', 'At base, conquest is not only the origin, it is also the crowning aim of all States, great or small, powerful or weak, despotic or liberal, monarchic, aristocratic, democratic, and even socialist, supposing that the ideal of the German socialists, that of a great communist State, is ever realized.

That it has been the point of departure for all States, ancient and modern, can be doubted by no one, since each page of universal history proves it sufficiently. No one contests any longer that the large current States have conquest for their more or less confessed aim. But the middling States and even the small ones, we are told, think only of defending themselves and it would be absurd on their part to dream of conquest.

Mock as much as you want, but nonetheless it is their dream, as it is the dream of the smallest peasant proprietor to increase to the detriment of his neighbor, to increase, to enlarge, to conquer always and at any price. It is a fatal tendency inherent in every State, whatever its extensions, its weakness or its strength, because it is a necessity of its nature. What is the State if it is not the organization of power; but it is in the nature of all power to not be able to tolerate either superiors or equals–power having no other object than domination, and domination being real only when everything that hinders it is subjugated. Mikhail Bakunin's rejection of state-regulated freedom and John Stuart Mill's principle of individual tolerance in their respective works present contrasting views on the role of the state and individual liberty. Here's a comparison of their perspectives:

### Bakunin's Perspective

1. **Rejection of the State:**
   - Bakunin fundamentally opposes the state, viewing it as an instrument of oppression and a means of domination. He argues that the state is inherently hierarchical and that its existence is a negation of individual freedom.
   - In "The Principle of the State," Bakunin states that the state's primary aim is conquest and expansion, which he sees as a threat to individual liberty. He emphasizes that the state is an organization of power that seeks to dominate and subjugate others.

2. **Collectivism and Freedom:**
   - Bakunin advocates for a form of collectivism where individuals are free from state control. He believes that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state and the establishment of a decentralized, voluntary association of individuals.
   - He argues that the state is a tool used by the ruling class to maintain their power and that the freedom of the individual is compromised when the state exists.

3. **Social Organization:**
   - Bakunin sees social organization as a natural and necessary aspect of human life, but he believes that it should be based on voluntary associations and mutual aid rather than state coercion.
   - He argues that the state is an artificial construct that hinders the natural development of human freedom and that true freedom can only be achieved through the collective action of free individuals.

### Mill's Perspective

1. **Individual Liberty:**
   - Mill's "On Liberty" focuses on the importance of individual freedom and the need for a society that respects and protects individual rights. He argues that the state should not interfere with the actions of individuals unless those actions harm others.
   - Mill's principle of individual tolerance is based on the idea that the best way to achieve a good society is to allow individuals to pursue their own interests and desires, as long as they do not infringe on the rights of others.

2. **Limited State Intervention:**
   - Mill advocates for a limited state that intervenes only to protect individual rights and prevent harm to others. He believes that the state should not impose its will on individuals unless there is a clear and direct harm.
   - Mill's concept of "laissez-faire" (let do) is central to his argument, suggesting that the state should not interfere in the lives of individuals unless necessary.

3. **Social Contract:**
   - Mill acknowledges that individuals form a social contract, but he argues that this contract should be based on mutual respect and the protection of individual rights. He believes that the state should be a means to protect individual freedoms rather than a means of oppression.
   - Mill's view is that the state can play a positive role in society by protecting individual rights and promoting the common good, but it should not be an oppressive force.

### Key Differences

1. **Role of the State:**
   - **Bakunin:** Sees the state as an inherently oppressive institution that must be abolished.
   - **Mill:** Sees the state as a necessary institution that can play a positive role in protecting individual rights, but it should be limited and not overreach.

2. **Nature of Freedom:**
   - **Bakunin:** Views freedom as the absence of state control and the ability to act freely within a voluntary association.
   - **Mill:** Views freedom as the ability to act without interference from the state, as long as one does not harm others.

3. **Social Organization:**
   - **Bakunin:** Advocates for a decentralized, voluntary social organization.
   - **Mill:** Sees social organization as a natural part of human life but believes it should be based on mutual respect and the protection of individual rights.

In summary, while both thinkers advocate for individual freedom, Bakunin rejects the state entirely as an oppressive institution, whereas Mill sees the state as a necessary but limited institution that can protect individual rights.

In On Liberty, Mill argues that society gains far more by allowing individuals to live as seems good to themselves rather than compelling them to conform to collective standards. Both thinkers champion individual freedom over collective compulsion, though Mill focuses on social tolerance of personal choices, whereas Bakunin attacks state regulation itself as inherently illusory and oppressive.

Bakunin argues for the integration of manual and intellectual labor, stating that in a future society, there should be no distinction between workers and scholars, as both pursuits (muscular and nervous) must be developed equally. He believes that this integration will lead to more productive and fruitful work and science.

Both thinkers identify the division of mental and physical labor as a primary source of social inequality, agreeing that true emancipation requires reuniting intellectual and manual activity.

Karl Marx's formula for productive capital in Capital, Volume 2, is presented as P... C' — M' — C... P. This formula emphasizes the periodic nature of the productive process, where productive capital (P) undergoes a cycle of production (P... C' — M'), followed by the realization of surplus-value (M' — C... P), and then is renewed for the next cycle.

In contrast, John Stuart Mill's concept of capital reproduction in Principles of Political Economy is more focused on the broader social context of production and consumption. Mill discusses the annual product of society, which includes both the replacement of capital and the production of individual consumption. He notes that the annual product includes both the constant capital (C) and the variable capital (v) plus surplus-value (s), and that the process of reproduction involves both productive and individual consumption.

While Marx's formula is specific to the movement of industrial capital within the capitalist mode of production, Mill's discussion is broader, encompassing the entire social capital and its reproduction. Marx's formula highlights the periodicity and self-expansion of value, whereas Mill's analysis includes the distribution of the product among different social classes and the conditions under which simple reproduction occurs.

Mill does not provide a specific formula like Marx's, but his analysis of the annual product and its components (C' = C + c) aligns with the idea of capital reproduction, albeit in a more general and less formalized manner. Mill's focus is on the social aspects of capital reproduction, such as the distribution of the product and the relationship between labor and capital, rather than on the formal circuit of capital as Marx describes.
reference: In Capital, Volume 2, Marx formalizes the circuit of productive capital (P...C'-M'-C...P) to demonstrate how capital functions through periodic renewal and value-valorisation during production. In Principles of Political Economy, Mill similarly observes that capital is maintained not by static preservation, but by perpetual reproduction, as consumed goods are continuously replaced by newly produced equivalent values. Both economists recognize that capital is not a fixed asset but a dynamic process requiring continuous reproduction, though Marx formulates this through explicit circuit formulas of value expansion, while Mill focuses on the physical replacement of consumed wealth.

["... We have said that man is not only the most individualistic being on earth – he is also the most social. It was a great mistake on the part of Jean Jacques Rousseau to have thought that primitive society was established through a free agreement among savages. But Jean Jacques is not the only one to have said this. The majority of jurists and modern publicists, either of the school of Kant or any other individualist and liberal school, those who do not accept the idea of a society founded upon the divine right of the theologians nor of a society determined by the Hegelian school as a more or less mystical realisation of objective morality, nor of the naturalists' concept of a primitive animal society, all accept, nolens volens, and for lack of any other basis, the tacit agreement or contract as their starting point.

According to the theory of the social contract primitive men enjoying absolute liberty only in isolation are antisocial by nature. When forced to associate they destroy each other's freedom. If this struggle is unchecked it can lead to mutual extermination. In order not to destroy each other completely, they conclude a contract, formal or tacit, whereby they surrender some of their freedom to assure the rest. This contract becomes the foundation of society, or rather of the State, for we must point out that in this theory there is no place for society; only the State exists, or rather society is completely absorbed by the State.", 'Any logical and straightforward theory of the State is essentially founded upon the principle of authority, that is, the eminently theological, metaphysical, and political idea that the masses, always incapable of governing themselves, must at all times submit to the beneficent yoke of a wisdom and a justice imposed upon them, in some way or other, from above. Imposed in the name of what, and by whom? Authority which is recognised and respected as such by the masses can come from three sources only: force, religion, or the action of a superior intelligence. As we are discussing the theory of the State founded upon the free contract, we must postpone discussion of those states founded on the dual authority of religion and force and, for the moment, confine our attention to authority based upon a superior intelligence, which is, as we know, always represented by minorities.

What do we really see in all states past and present, even those endowed with the most democratic institutions, such as the United States of North America and Switzerland? Actual self-government of the masses, despite the pretence that the people hold all the power, remains a fiction most of the time. It is always, in fact, minorities that do the governing. In the United States, up to the recent Civil War and partly even now, and even within the party of the present incumbent, President Andrew Johnson, those ruling minorities were the so-called Democrats, who continued to favour slavery and the ferocious oligarchy of the Southern planters, demagogues without faith or conscience, capable of sacrificing everything to their greed, to their malignant ambition. They were those who, through their detestable actions, and influence, exercised practically without opposition for almost fifty successive years, have greatly contributed to the corruption of political morality in North America.', "Thus the State, like the Church, starts out with this fundamental supposition, that men are basically evil, and that, if delivered up to their natural liberty, they would tear each other apart and offer the spectacle of the most terrifying anarchy, where the stronger would exploit and slaughter the weaker – quite the contrary of what goes on in our model states today, needless to say! The State sets up the principle that in order to establish public order, there is need of a superior authority; in order to guide men and repress their evil passions, there is need of a guide and a curb.

. . . In order to assure the observance of the principles and the administration of laws in any human society whatsoever, there has to be a vigilant, regulating, and, if need be, repressive power at the head of the State. It remains for us to find out who should and who could exercise such power.

For the State founded upon divine right and through the intervention of any God whatever, the answer is simple enough; the men to exercise such power would be the priests primarily, and secondarily the temporal authorities consecrated by the priests. For the State founded on the free social contract, the answer would be far more difficult. In a pure democracy of equals – all of whom are, however, considered incapable of self-restraint on behalf of the common welfare, their liberty tending naturally toward evil – who would be the true guardian and administrator of the laws, the defender of justice and of public order against everyone's evil passions? In a word, who would fulfil the functions of the State?", 'It is the same with the State founded upon the theory of the social contract. According to this principle, the good and the just commence only with the contract; they are, in fact, nothing but the very contents and the purpose of the contract; that is, the common interest and the public right of all the individuals who have formed the contract among themselves, with the exclusion of all those who remain outside the contract. It is; consequently, nothing but the greatest satisfaction given to the collective egotism of a special and restricted association, which, being founded upon the partial sacrifice of the individual egotism of each of its members, rejects from its midst, as strangers and natural enemies, the immense majority of the human species, whether or not it may be organised into analogous organisation.

The existence of one sovereign, exclusionary State necessarily supposes the existence and, if need be, provokes the formation of other such States, since it is quite natural that individuals who find themselves outside it and are threatened by it in their existence and in their liberty, should, in their turn, associate themselves against it. We thus have humanity divided into an indefinite number of foreign states, all hostile and threatened by each other. There is no common right, no social contract of any kind between them; otherwise they would cease to be independent states and become the federated members of one great state. But unless this great state were to embrace all of humanity, it would be confronted with other great states, each federated within, each maintaining the same posture of inevitable hostility. War would still remain the supreme law, an unavoidable condition of human survival.

Every state, federated or not, would therefore seek to become the most powerful. It must devour lest it be devoured, conquer lest it be conquered, enslave lest it be enslaved, since two powers, similar and yet alien to each other, could not coexist without mutual destruction.', 'Produced by Curtis A. All speculations concerning forms of government bear the impress, more
or less exclusive, of two conflicting theories respecting political

By some minds, government is conceived as strictly a practical art,
giving rise to no questions but those of means and an end. Forms of

to be worked like any other question of business. The first step is to

Bakunin critiques this view, stating that the state is fundamentally based on the idea of authority, which is often exercised by minorities over the majority. Bakunin argues that the state is inherently hierarchical and exclusionary, leading to a division of humanity into competing states that are in a constant state of hostility and conflict.

In contrast, John Stuart Mill's view in "Considerations on Representative Government" does not focus on the origin of the state but rather on its functions and forms. Mill discusses the idea of government as a practical art, where the form of government can be chosen based on the purposes it aims to fulfill. He suggests that the best form of government is one that maximizes the greatest amount of good with the least of evil, and that this can be determined through a process of inquiry and persuasion among the people.

Thus, while Bakunin critiques the Rousseauian state as inherently oppressive and exclusionary, Mill views government as a tool that can be shaped to serve the common good, provided it is properly constituted and its representatives are accountable to the people.
reference: In Rousseau's Theory of the State, Bakunin rejects social contract origins, contending that the state arose from violence, conquest, and plunder, and persists purely through coercive force. In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill treats government functionally as an instrument to be evaluated by its adaptation to social ends, identifying the virtue and intelligence of citizens as its prime element. While Bakunin views the state as an inherently violent institution rooted in historical plunder, Mill evaluates government as a malleable tool for promoting civic development and public utility.

Karl Marx's description of the Paris Commune in "The Civil War in France" and Mikhail Bakunin's organizational principles in "The Organization of the International" present contrasting views on the nature of the state and the role of the working class.

Marx describes the Paris Commune as the "Dictatorship of the Proletariat," emphasizing that it was a form of state power that the working class must exercise to overthrow the existing state. He notes that the Commune was a temporary measure, a necessary evil that would be discarded once a new generation could abolish the state. Marx criticizes the Proudhon school of socialism, which advocated for small-scale associations and opposed large-scale state intervention, arguing that the Commune's measures, such as the organization of large-scale industry, were necessary steps towards communism.

In contrast, Bakunin's organizational principles in "The Organization of the International" emphasize the importance of the working class organizing from the bottom up, based on their real interests and natural instincts. He argues that the International should not aim to create a new state but to destroy existing government systems. Bakunin's view is that the state is inherently oppressive and that the working class should organize independently of the state to achieve their goals.

While both Marx and Bakunin recognize the need for the working class to organize, they differ significantly in their views on the nature of the state and the role of the International. Marx sees the state as a tool to be used temporarily, while Bakunin sees it as an enemy to be completely abolished.

In The Organization of the International, Bakunin asserts that the working class must organize from below upward through free federations of autonomous trade sections and communes. Both authors champion decentralized, bottom-up organization by workers, though Marx emphasizes direct electoral accountability within municipal bodies, whereas Bakunin insists on complete autonomy for federated trade unions and local sections without state-like representation.

Political Freedom without economic equality is a pretense, a fraud, a lie; and the workers want no lying.

It is the real, living internationalism of labor.', '<2-hop: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, Manifesto of the Communist Party> The Communists are further reproached with desiring to abolish countries and nationality. response:
Bakunin's concept of worker solidarity in "The Red Association" emphasizes the international nature of the workers' movement and the need for workers to unite across national boundaries. He argues that the emancipation of the worker is an international question and that the solution can only be achieved through an international movement. Bakunin states that the Council Association should federate from below and speak in every group of workers, aiming for a common solidarity of movement that transcends national borders.

In contrast, Marx and Engels' declaration on nationality in the Manifesto of the Communist Party acknowledges the historical context of 1847, where Russia and the United States were not yet significant parts of the proletarian movement. They note that the Manifesto, while a historical document, should not be altered and that its principles should guide the international working class movement. However, the Manifesto itself does not explicitly discuss nationality in the same way Bakunin does in "The Red Association."

Bakunin's view is more explicitly internationalist, while the Manifesto's approach to nationality is more about recognizing the historical context and the evolving nature of the workers' movement. Bakunin's emphasis on the Council Association as a means to achieve international worker solidarity is a key aspect of his philosophy, whereas the Manifesto's treatment of nationality is more about the limitations of the time it was written.
reference: In The Red Association, Bakunin defines worker internationalism as the active solidarity of laborers across all trades and countries against capitalist exploitation. In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels famously declare that working men have no country, rejecting national allegiance under capitalist exploitation. Both texts reject national divisions among the proletariat in favor of global working-class unity against capital, agreeing that shared economic exploitation unites workers beyond national boundaries.

#notes Source: Bakunin on Anarchy, translated and edited by Sam Dolgoff, 1971. Man, Society and Freedom is taken from a long, unfinished note to The Knouto-Germanic Empire and the Social Revolution, actually penned by Bakunin’s close associates Carlo Cafiero and Élisée Reclus in 1871, the same work from which God and State is taken.



The doctrinaire liberals, reasoning from the premises of individual freedom, pose as the adversaries of the State. Those among them who maintain that the government, i.e., the body of functionaries organized and designated to perform the functions of the State is a
necessary evil,
and that the progress of civilization consists in always and continuously diminishing the attributes and the rights of the States, are inconsistent. Such is the theory, but in practice these same doctrinaire liberals, when the existence or the stability of the State is seriously threatened, are just as fanatical defenders of the State as are the monarchists and the Jacobins.', 'Man completely realizes his individual freedom as well as his personality only through the individuals who surround him, and thanks only to the labor and the collective power of society. Without society he would surely remain the most stupid and the most miserable among all the other ferocious beasts.... Society, far from decreasing his freedom, on the contrary creates the individual freedom of all human beings. Society is the root, the tree, and liberty is its fruit. Hence, in every epoch, man must seek his freedom not at the beginning but at the end of history. It can be said that the real and complete emancipation of every individual is the true, the great, the supreme aim of history....

The materialistic. realistic, and collectivist conception of freedom, as opposed to the idealistic, is this: Man becomes conscious of himself and his humanity only in society and only by the collective action of the whole society. He frees himself from the yoke of external nature only by collective and social labor, which alone can transform the earth into an abode favorable to the development of humanity. Without such material emancipation the intellectual and moral emancipation of the individual is impossible. He can emancipate himself from the yoke of his own nature, i.e. subordinate his instincts and the movements of his body to the conscious direction of his mind, the development of which is fostered only by education and training. But education and training are preeminently and exclusively social ... hence the isolated individual cannot possibly become conscious of his freedom.

To be free ... means to be acknowledged and treated as such by all his fellowmen. The liberty of every individual is only the reflection of his own humanity, or his human right through the conscience of all free men, his brothers and his equals.', 'I am truly free only when all human beings, men and women, are equally free. The freedom of other men, far from negating or limiting my freedom, is, on the contrary, its necessary premise and confirmation. It is the slavery of other men that sets up a barrier to my freedom, or what amounts to the same thing, it is their bestiality which is the negation of my humanity. For my dignity as a man, my human right which consists of refusing to obey any other man, and to determine my own acts in conformity with my convictions is reflected by the equally free conscience of all and confirmed by the consent of all humanity. My personal freedom, confirmed by the liberty of all, extends to infinity.

The materialistic conception of freedom is therefore a very positive, very complex thing, and above all, eminently social, because it can be realized only in society and by the strictest equality and solidarity among all men. One can distinguish the main elements in the attainment of freedom. The first is eminently social. It is the fullest development of all the faculties and powers of every human being, by education, by scientific training, and by material prosperity; things which can only be provided for every individual by the collective, material, intellectual, manual, and sedentary labor of society in general.

The second element of freedom is negative. It is the revolt of the individual against all divine, collective, and individual authority.', 'In addition to this practical reason, there is still another of a theoretical nature which also leads even the most sincere liberals back to the cult of the State. They consider themselves liberals because their theory on the origin of society is based on the principle of individual freedom, and it is precisely because of this that they must inevitably recognize the absolute right [sovereignty] of the State.

According to them individual freedom is not a creation, a historic product of society. They maintain, on the contrary, that individual freedom is anterior to all society and that all men are endowed by God with an immortal soul. Man is accordingly a complete being, absolutely independent, apart from and outside society. In short, according to this theory, individuals are not the product of society but, on the contrary, are led to create society by some necessity such as work or war.

It follows from this theory that society, strictly speaking, does not exist. The natural human society, the beginning of all civilization, the only milieu in which the personality and the liberty of man is formed and developed does not exist for them. On the one hand, this theory recognizes only self — sufficient individuals living in isolation, and on the other hand, only a society arbitrarily created by them and based only on a formal or tacit contract, i.e., on the State. their own special claims and responsibilities; that they deliberately

_To the beloved and deplored memory of her who was the inspirer, and in

single personality possesses in a modern world do not belong to him by

His virtue lies in recognising the intimate communion with his fellows.

reference_contexts: ['<1-hop: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty> He who lets the world, or his own portion of it, choose his plan of life for him, has no need of any other faculty than the ape-like one of imitation. He who chooses his plan for himself, employs all his faculties.', '<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, Man, Society, and Freedom> Man becomes conscious of himself and his humanity only in society and only by the collective action of the whole society... Individual freedom is not a solitary fact, but a collective product.']
response:
John Stuart Mill emphasizes individual self-determination as a fundamental aspect of liberty. He argues that individuals have inherent rights that should not be infringed upon by society, and that true freedom is achieved when individuals are not coerced by others, including the state. Mill believes that individuals are naturally prior to the state and that their liberties are not forfeited when they form a social contract.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin views freedom as a collective and social phenomenon. He argues that individual freedom is realized through the collective power of society and that the true freedom of an individual is confirmed by the freedom of all. Bakunin sees the state as an obstacle to individual freedom and believes that true freedom can only be achieved through the abolition of the state and the establishment of a free association of individuals.

Bakunin's view is that individual freedom is not something that exists independently of society but is dependent on the collective freedom of all. He sees the state as a tool of oppression that limits individual freedom, and thus, the goal should be the complete abolition of the state to achieve true freedom for all individuals. Mill, on the other hand, acknowledges the importance of society but maintains that individuals have inherent rights that should be protected from the state and other individuals.
reference: In On Liberty, Mill stresses individual self-determination, warning that letting others choose one's life plan reduces human action to mere ape-like imitation rather than full faculty development. In Man, Society, and Freedom, Bakunin maintains that human consciousness and individual freedom are not solitary facts, but collective products generated through social action. While Mill focuses on shielding individual self-choice from social pressure, Bakunin emphasizes that individual personality and freedom can only emerge through collective social existence.

Based on the provided context, Karl Marx's critique of Proudhon in "Poverty of Philosophy" and John Stuart Mill's critique of philosophical abstractions in "Auguste Comte and Positivism" share some similarities but also differ in their focus and approach.

Marx's critique of Proudhon is rooted in economic and philosophical differences. Marx argues that Proudhon's work, while claiming to be a comprehensive treatise, is actually a collection of mystical and abstract ideas that lack a solid economic foundation. Marx sees Proudhon's work as overly philosophical and lacking in practical economic analysis, which Marx believes is crucial for understanding and addressing social issues.

In contrast, Mill's critique of Auguste Comte's positivism focuses on the abstract nature of Comte's philosophy and its lack of practical application. Mill criticizes Comte for elevating certain philosophical concepts to a level of absolute truth, such as the "Sovereignty of the People," which Mill sees as overly negative and impractical. Mill argues that such abstractions can hinder the development of positive science and practical social reform.

Both Marx and Mill critique the tendency to rely on philosophical abstractions, but they do so from different perspectives. Marx is more concerned with the economic implications of Proudhon's ideas, while Mill is more focused on the practical utility and scientific rigor of Comte's positivism.

In summary, while both critiques target the overreliance on philosophical abstractions, Marx's critique is more economic in nature, focusing on Proudhon's lack of practical economic analysis, whereas Mill's critique is more philosophical and scientific, focusing on the impracticality of Comte's absolute principles.
reference: In Poverty of Philosophy, Marx criticizes Proudhon for turning economic relations upside down by treating abstract theoretical categories as real entities rather than expressions of social production. In Auguste Comte and Positivism, Mill similarly warns against the philosophical error of mistaking abstractions for independent entities separate from concrete phenomena. Both thinkers condemn the fallacy of reification—treating mental abstractions as real generating forces—and insist that concepts must remain grounded in actual empirical and social realities.

John Stuart Mill's justification for free speech in "On Liberty" and Mikhail Bakunin's view of intellectual liberty in "What is Authority" share some commonalities but also have significant differences.

Mill argues for the importance of free speech and thought as essential for human development and the richness of society. He states that the "grand, leading principle" of his argument is the "absolute and essential importance of human development in its richest diversity." Mill believes that the suppression of individual thought and expression can stifle the progress of society and the potential for new ideas. He sees free speech as a means to ensure that the best ideas can emerge and contribute to the common good.

In contrast, Bakunin's view of intellectual liberty is more critical of authority and the potential for intellectual elites to impose their will. Bakunin distinguishes between the "absolute authority of science" and the "infallibility and universality of the representatives of science." He sees the latter as a form of authority that can be oppressive and false. Bakunin advocates for the rejection of any official or privileged authority, including that of science, and instead supports the acceptance of scientific knowledge as a natural authority.

While both authors value intellectual freedom, Mill sees it as a means to foster societal progress and the flourishing of diverse ideas, whereas Bakunin views it as a way to challenge and reject oppressive authority structures, including those that claim infallibility.
reference: In On Liberty, Mill defends absolute freedom of opinion, arguing that silencing even a single dissenting voice robs humanity of the opportunity to discover truth or challenge dogma. In What is Authority?, Bakunin accepts voluntary deference to specialized technical expertise in specific domains, but firmly rejects allowing any expert or authority to impose their will upon him. While Mill focuses on protecting free expression against social and political censorship, Bakunin distinguishes between voluntary, functional consultation of experts and compulsory authority.

response:
According to Marx in Capital, Volume 1, surplus value is not seen as arising from the productivity of labor, but rather as a result of the exploitation of labor by capital. Marx argues that the capitalist mode of production inherently generates surplus value through the appropriation of the surplus labor of workers, which is not compensated in full by their wages. He criticizes John Stuart Mill for conflating the productivity of labor with the origin of surplus value, stating that Mill's view is a repetition of earlier vulgar economic errors.

In contrast, John Stuart Mill in Principles of Political Economy presents a view where the productivity of labor is seen as a key factor in the generation of profit. Mill states that "the cause of profit is that labour produces more than is required for its support." However, Marx criticizes this view as incomplete and potentially misleading, suggesting that Mill's perspective does not adequately address the exploitative nature of capitalist production.

Marx further argues that the accumulation of capital is not simply a result of saving and investment, but is driven by the need to exploit labor and expand the means of production. He criticizes the idea that capital accumulation can occur without a prior increase in production, pointing out that this view fails to recognize the exploitative relationship at the heart of capitalist production.

In summary, Marx views surplus value as a product of capitalist exploitation, while Mill sees it as a result of labor productivity, though Marx criticizes this view for not fully addressing the exploitative nature of capitalism.
reference: In Capital, Volume 1, Marx defines surplus-value as the direct measure of capital's exploitation of labor power, asserting that social economic forms differ primarily in how surplus-labor is extracted from producers. In Principles of Political Economy, Mill treats capital accumulation as the product of individual abstinence and saving, where unconsumed income is advanced to productive laborers who reproduce it with a profit. While Marx views capital accumulation as driven by structural surplus-labor extraction, Mill explains it as voluntary saving and productive advance.

response:
Mikhail Bakunin's proposal for revolutionary destruction in "Principles and Organization of the International Revolutionary Society" and Karl Marx's view of legislative reform in "Critique of the Gotha Programme" present two distinct approaches to achieving a socialist society. Here are the key contrasts:

### Bakunin's Revolutionary Destruction

1. **Nature of the State and Authority**:
   - **Bakunin**: Views the State as an inherently oppressive and authoritarian institution that must be destroyed. He sees the State as the primary obstacle to the natural development and freedom of the people.
   - **Marx**: Acknowledges the State as a necessary transitional institution but believes it will wither away as class distinctions disappear. He sees the State as a tool for the dictatorship of the proletariat, which will eventually lead to a classless society.

2. **Role of the International**:
   - **Bakunin**: Proposes a decentralized, non-hierarchical organization of the International that aims to influence the masses through natural, unofficial means. He emphasizes the importance of industrial organization and the natural instincts of the people.
   - **Marx**: Sees the International as a means to propagate revolutionary ideas and organize the working class. He advocates for a more structured and disciplined approach to achieve the goals of the proletariat.

3. **Means to Achieve Goals**:
   - **Bakunin**: Emphasizes the use of direct action, insurrection, and the spontaneous uprising of the masses. He believes in the power of the people to overthrow the State through their own efforts.
   - **Marx**: Advocates for a more gradual and legislative approach, emphasizing the need for a proletarian party to lead the revolution and implement socialist policies through the state apparatus.

4. **Role of the Proletariat**:
   - **Bakunin**: Views the proletariat as a class that will naturally rebel against the State and oppressive conditions. He sees the International as a means to channel and organize this natural rebellion.
   - **Marx**: Sees the proletariat as a class that needs to be organized and educated to understand its true interests and the need for a socialist revolution. He emphasizes the importance of a vanguard party to guide the proletariat.

### Legislative Reform in Critique of the Gotha Programme

1. **Nature of the State**:
   - **Marx**: While critical of the existing state, he sees it as a necessary tool for the dictatorship of the proletariat. He believes that the state will eventually wither away as class distinctions disappear.

2. **Role of the Party**:
   - **Marx**: Emphasizes the role of a proletarian party to lead the revolution and implement socialist policies. He sees the party as a disciplined and organized force that can guide the proletariat towards its goals.

3. **Means to Achieve Goals**:
   - **Marx**: Advocates for a combination of political action, legislative reforms, and the use of the state apparatus to achieve socialist goals. He sees the state as a means to implement socialist policies and eventually transition to a classless society.

4. **Role of the Proletariat**:
   - **Marx**: Sees the proletariat as a class that needs to be organized and educated to understand its true interests and the need for a socialist revolution. He emphasizes the importance of a vanguard party to guide the proletariat.

### Summary

- **Bakunin** focuses on the immediate destruction of the State and the spontaneous uprising of the masses, while **Marx** advocates for a more structured and legislative approach, emphasizing the role of a vanguard party to guide the proletariat towards its goals.
- **Bakunin** sees the International as a means to channel and organize the natural rebellion of the people, whereas **Marx** views it as a tool for propagating revolutionary ideas and organizing the working class.
- **Bakunin** believes in the power of direct action and insurrection, while **Marx** advocates for a combination of political action and legislative reforms.

These differences reflect the broader ideological divide between anarchism and Marxism, with Bakunin advocating for a more radical and immediate approach to revolution, and Marx proposing a more gradual and structured path to achieving a socialist society.

In Critique of the Gotha Programme, Marx maintains that between capitalist and communist society lies a necessary political transition period in which the state takes the form of the revolutionary dictatorship of the proletariat. While Bakunin insists that preserving any state machinery prevents freedom, Marx sees a temporary revolutionary state as essential for social transformation.

response:
Bakunin and Marx both critique the state bureaucracy and executive power, but their perspectives differ significantly.

Bakunin, in "Statism and Anarchy," views the state bureaucracy as an instrument of oppression that must be destroyed. He argues that the state machinery has become independent of civil society, with the state power representing a class, specifically the peasants, rather than the working class. Bakunin fears that if the state is used to achieve proletarian revolution, it will either become indistinguishable from bourgeois parties or, if it comes to power, will form a new ruling elite, mirroring what he sees as the potential for a "dictatorship of the proletariat" to become a new form of oppression.

Marx, in "The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte," describes the state bureaucracy as an instrument of the ruling class, which can sometimes appear to gain independence from the bourgeoisie. He notes that under the second Bonaparte, the state machinery had strengthened itself to such an extent that it could be represented by a single individual, Louis Bonaparte, who was an outsider and a symbol of the peasants' interests. Marx sees the state as a tool that can be manipulated by different classes, but ultimately serves the interests of the dominant class. He critiques the state's role in suppressing the working class and the peasantry, and he views the coup d'état as a means by which the state can be used to maintain the status quo or to impose a new form of class rule.

In summary, while both authors see the state bureaucracy as a tool of oppression, Bakunin emphasizes the need for its complete destruction, whereas Marx sees it as a more complex instrument that can be used by different classes to maintain their power.
reference: In Statism and Anarchy, Bakunin maintains that every government inherently positions itself above the populace, with its state bureaucracy acting as a privileged caste that lives off public labor. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, Marx similarly describes the French executive power as an enormous parasitic body with military and bureaucratic machinery that arose during absolute monarchy to enmesh society. Both thinkers portray state bureaucracy as an alien, parasitic institution standing above society, though Marx traces its specific historical emergence under monarchical centralization while Bakunin treats it as an inherent property of all state rule.

According to the provided context, John Stuart Mill and Karl Marx have contrasting views on capitalist competition:

John Stuart Mill in "Principles of Political Economy" argues that competition in markets is beneficial. He states that competition keeps prices from falling too low, as both buyers and sellers compete. Mill acknowledges that in some cases, a single large company might be better than multiple smaller ones, but generally, he sees competition as leading to lower prices and better service for consumers. He does not see competition as inherently exploitative or leading to monopolies that harm the laboring classes.

In contrast, Karl Marx in "Capital, Volume 1" views competition as part of the capitalist mode of production that exploits the working class. Marx does not explicitly quote from his own work in the provided context, but based on his critique of political economy, he would likely argue that competition does not benefit workers but rather large capitalists who can drive out smaller competitors. Marx would see competition as a mechanism for concentrating capital and increasing exploitation of labor.

In Capital, Volume 1, Marx analyzes competition as a coercive battle fought through commodity cheapening, where larger capitals inevitably crush smaller ones through economies of scale and increased labor productivity. While Mill views competition as a beneficial moral and practical driver of human development, Marx analyzes it as a structural law driving capital concentration and centralisation.

Mikhail Bakunin's rejection of religious morality in "God and the State" and John Stuart Mill's advocacy of utilitarian morality in "Utilitarianism" can be compared as follows:

1. **Bakunin's Rejection of Religious Morality:**
   - Bakunin argues against the idea of a divine authority and the concept of a "divine justice" that supersedes human justice. He suggests that the belief in a divine authority is a tool used by those in power to maintain control over the masses.
   - Bakunin emphasizes that all forms of power, including those derived from religion, are subject to critical examination and should be dismantled. He believes that human justice should replace divine justice.
   - Bakunin's view is rooted in a materialist perspective, where he sees ideas and beliefs as products of material conditions and social structures.

2. **Mill's Utilitarian Morality:**
   - Mill advocates for a form of utilitarianism, which he defines as the principle that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.
   - Mill argues that the ultimate criterion for morality is the greatest happiness for the greatest number. He believes that moral rules and principles should be judged based on their utility in promoting overall happiness.
   - Mill's utilitarianism is more focused on the practical application of ethical principles and the consequences of actions, rather than on abstract theological or metaphysical arguments.

3. **Key Differences:**
   - **Source of Morality:** Bakunin rejects the idea of divine or religious authority as a source of morality, while Mill sees utility as a practical and empirical basis for moral judgments.
   - **Scope of Application:** Bakunin's critique is more focused on the political and social structures that derive from religious authority, whereas Mill's utilitarianism is a broader ethical framework applicable to individual and collective actions.
   - **Methodology:** Bakunin's approach is more revolutionary and calls for the overthrow of existing power structures, while Mill's utilitarianism is more about reforming and improving existing social and moral practices.

In summary, while both Bakunin and Mill reject traditional religious justifications for morality, they do so for different reasons and propose different methods for establishing a new moral order. Bakunin's rejection is more radical and calls for the dismantling of all forms of authority, whereas Mill's utilitarianism seeks to reform and improve society through practical ethical considerations.

While Bakunin views religious belief as fundamentally incompatible with human freedom and dignity, Mill integrates traditional moral teachings into his utilitarian framework for promoting social happiness.

user_input: How does John Stuart Mill's view of representative democracy in Considerations on Representative Government contrast with Mikhail Bakunin's assessment of representative voting in The Illusion of Universal Suffrage?
retrieved_contexts:
["Men once believed that the establishment of universal suffrage would guarantee the freedom of the peoples. That, alas, was a great illusion, and the realization of that illusion has led in many places to the downfall and demoralization of the radical party. The radicals did not wish to deceive the people—or so the liberal papers assure us—but in that case they were certainly themselves deceived. They were genuinely convinced when they promised the people freedom through universal suffrage, and inspired by that conviction they were able to arouse the masses and overthrow the established aristocratic governments. Today, having learnt from experience and power politics, they have lost faith in themselves and in their own principles and in that way they have sunk into defeat and corruption. Yet the whole thing seemed so natural and so simple; once legislative and executive power emanated directly from a popular election, must it not become the pure expression of the people's will, and could that will produce anything other than freedom and well-being among the populace?

The whole deception of the representative system lies in the fiction that a government and a legislature emerging out of a popular election must or even can represent the real will of the people. Instinctively and inevitably the people expect two things: the greatest possible material prosperity combined with the greatest freedom of movement and action: that means the best organization of popular economic interests, and the complete absence of any kind of power or political organization—since all political organization is destined to end in the negation of freedom. Such are the basic longings of the people.", "In Switzerland, as elsewhere, the ruling class is completely different and separate from the mass of the governed. Here, as everywhere, no matter how egalitarian our political constitution may be, it is the bourgeoisie who rule, and it is the people—workers and peasants—who obey their laws. The people have neither the leisure nor the necessary education to occupy themselves with government. Since the bourgeoisie have both, they have, in fact if not by right, exclusive privilege. Thus, in Switzerland as elsewhere, political equality is merely a puerile fiction, a lie. But how, separated as they are from the people by all the economic and social circumstances of their existence, can the bourgeoisie express, in laws and in government, the feelings, ideas and wishes of the people? It is impossible, and daily experience in fact proves that, in legislation as well as government, the bourgeoisie is mainly directed by its own interests and prejudices, without any great concern for those of the people. It is true that all our legislators, as well as all the members of cantonal governments, are elected, directly or indirectly, by the people. It is true that on elect.ion day even the proudest of bourgeoisie, if they have any political ambitions, are obliged to pay court to Her Majesty, the Sovereign People ... But once the elections are over, the people return to their work and the bourgeoisie to their profitable businesses and political intrigues. They neither meet nor recognize each other again. And how can one expect the people, burdened by their work and ignorant for the most part of current problems, to supervise the political actions of their representatives? In reality, the control exercised by voters on their elected representatives is a pure fiction. But since, in the representative system, popular control is the only guarantee of the people's freedom, it is quite evident that such freedom in its turn is no more than a fiction.", "The instincts of the rulers, whether they legislate or execute the laws, are—by the very fact of their exceptional position—diametrically opposite. However democratic may be their feelings and their intentions, 'once they achieve the elevation of office they can only view society in the same way as a schoolmaster views his pupils, and between pupils and masters equality cannot exist. On one side there is the feeling of superiority that is inevitably provoked by a position of superiority; on the other side, there is the sense of inferiority which follows from the superiority of the teacher, whether he is exercising an executive or a legislative power. Who-ever talks of political power talks of domination; but where domination exists there is inevitably a somewhat large section of society that is dominated, and those who are dominated quite naturally detest their dominators, while the dominators have no choice but to subdue and oppress those they dominate. This is the eternal history of political power, ever since that power has appeared in the world. This is what also explains why and how the most extreme of democrats, the most raging rebels, become. the most cautious of conservatives as soon as they attain to power. Such recantations are usually regarded as acts of treason, but that is an error; their main cause is simply the change of position and hence of perspective...", 'The common mode of attempting this is by limiting the democratic
character of the representation through a more or less restricted
suffrage. But there is a previous consideration which, duly kept in
view, considerably modifies the circumstances which are supposed to
render such a restriction necessary. A completely equal democracy, in
a nation in which a single class composes the numerical majority, can
not be divested of certain evils; but those evils are greatly
aggravated by the fact that the democracies which at present exist are
not equal, but systematically unequal in favor of the predominant
class. Two very different ideas are usually confounded under the name
democracy. The pure idea of democracy, according to its definition, is
the government of the whole people by the whole people, equally
represented. Democracy, as commonly conceived and hitherto practiced,
is the government of the whole people by a mere majority of the people
exclusively represented. The former is synonymous with the equality of
all citizens; the latter, strangely confounded with it, is a
government of privilege in favor of the numerical majority, who alone
possess practically any voice in the state. This is the inevitable
consequence of the manner in which the votes are now taken, to the
complete disfranchisement of minorities.', 'Produced by Curtis A. Weyant

Those who have done me the honor of reading my previous writings will
probably receive no strong impression of novelty from the present

Chapter I--To What Extent Forms of Government are a Matter of Choice.


All speculations concerning forms of government bear the impress, more
or less exclusive, of two conflicting theories respecting political
institutions; or, to speak more properly, conflicting conceptions of
what political institutions are.', 'I have discussed this question on the assumption that the electoral
system, in all that depends on positive institution, conforms to the
principles laid down in the preceding chapters. Even on this
hypothesis, the delegation theory of representation seems to me false,
and its practical operation hurtful, though the mischief would in that
case be confined within certain bounds. But if the securities by which
I have endeavoured to guard the representative principle are not
recognized by the Constitution; if provision is not made for the
representation of minorities, nor any difference admitted in the
numerical value of votes, according to some criterion of the amount of
education possessed by the voters--in that case, no words can
exaggerate the importance in principle of leaving an unfettered
discretion to the representative; for it would then be the only
chance, under universal suffrage, for any other opinions than those of
the majority to be heard in Parliament. In that falsely called
democracy which is really the exclusive rule of the operative classes,
all others being unrepresented and unheard, the only escape from class
legislation in its narrowest, and political ignorance in its most
dangerous form, would lie in such disposition as the uneducated might
have to choose educated representatives, and to defer to their
opinions. Some willingness to do this might reasonably be expected,
and every thing would depend upon cultivating it to the highest point.
But, once invested with political omnipotence, if the operative
classes voluntarily concurred in imposing in this or any other manner
any considerable limitation upon their self-opinion and self-will,
they would prove themselves wiser than any class possessed of absolute
power has shown itself, or, we may venture to say, is ever likely to

response:
John Stuart Mill and Mikhail Bakunin present contrasting views on representative democracy and universal suffrage.

Bakunin argues that universal suffrage is an illusion that has led to the downfall and corruption of radical parties. He believes that the people are naturally inclined to seek material prosperity and freedom, which cannot be achieved through a representative system. Bakunin also criticizes the representative system for being a fiction, as the elected representatives, particularly the bourgeoisie, are more concerned with their own interests rather than the people's. He contends that political power inherently leads to domination, and thus, the people are inevitably dominated by their representatives.

In contrast, Mill advocates for a form of representative democracy where the majority is represented, but he also emphasizes the importance of equal representation. Mill criticizes the current form of democracy as systematically unequal in favor of the predominant class, which he believes leads to the disfranchisement of minorities. He supports the idea of a more equal democracy where all citizens are equally represented. Mill also discusses the need for a second chamber to provide a check on the majority and ensure that the interests of minorities are also considered.

In summary, while Bakunin sees universal suffrage as inherently flawed and leading to corruption, Mill believes in a more equitable form of representation that can protect minority interests within a democratic framework.
reference: In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill defends representative democracy as a system that combines popular participation with expert governance, granting ultimate control to the people while placing management in trained hands. In contrast, Bakunin argues in The Illusion of Universal Suffrage that voting under economic inequality is a pure illusion that gives workers a momentary illusion of power while leaving their economic servitude intact. While Mill sees representative voting as an effective mechanism for democratic accountability, Bakunin considers political elections powerless without prior economic emancipation.

['Interestingly enough, Marx, who had learned Russian in order to study Russian economic conditions, carefully read
Statism and Anarchy.
Sometime in 1874–75 he went through the work and made lengthy extracts and notes. His own comments on it are few but revealing. His chief criticism of Bakunin was that he did not pay enough attention to the economic preconditions of revolution. “Will,” Marx complained, “not economic conditions, is the basis of his social revolution.” There was much to be said for this judgment. What Marx did not perceive so clearly was that precisely the opposite criticism might be leveled against him. His only response to Bakunin’s warning that socialism might produce a new ruling elite was to reiterate confidently that once economic conditions were changed and class rule came to an end, the state and all relations of political authority would necessarily disappear.[31] He would not entertain the possibility that political domination was a product of will, and not solely of economic conditions, and that the former might persist even after the latter had been transformed.

It is in the attack on Marx that the literary artistry of
Statism and Anarchy
reveals itself. The discussion of Marx and his views appears only in the last third of the book. By the time Bakunin gets to Marx, however, he has so identified the Germans with “statism” that Marx’s political outlook takes on a truly sinister cast. In the context which
Statism and Anarchy
has created, Marx becomes a kind of socialist Bismarck, promoting pan-German hegemony by other means. Whatever the fairness or accuracy of such a depiction – and it should be kept in mind that Marx, Lassalle, and the new German Social-Democratic Party, all of whom Bakunin lumps together, actually held different views on many issues – it is the product of a degree of literary skill for which Bakunin is rarely given credit.', 'Equally repellent, though less marked in this work than in some others, is Bakunin’s anti-Semitism, which often appeared as a corollary to his anti-Germanism. Again, it is in part a weapon in his war against Marx. Not only was Marx himself Jewish as well as German, but some of those who helped him in his campaign against Bakunin were also Jewish. Bakunin’s anti-Semitism, however, long antedated his conflict with Marx. It may be argued that such sentiments, however distasteful, do not negate Bakunin’s anarchist principles.[29] It may also be argued that those principles are somehow deficient if even one so passionately committed to them was unable to surmount crude ethnic prejudices. The most that can be said for Bakunin is that he was hardly unique in this regard. In France, for example, at least until the Dreyfus affair, socialist and anarchist writers and artists frequently employed stereotypical anti-Semitic images of the Jew as capitalist or banker, or simply as a crude synonym for “bourgeois.”[30] It should be noted also that Bakunin’s consistent (though not uncritical) support and defense of the Poles – in regard to whom so many otherwise liberal Russians had a moral blind spot – was a remarkable example of adherence to principle.

The second major theme of
Statism and Anarchy
is its critique of Marxism. To the Marxists, the proletariat’s participation in the political life of its respective nations seemed an effective way of pursuing the class struggle and ultimately achieving the supremacy of the proletariat and the elimination of the state. To the anarchists, however, any participation in “bourgeois politics” was inherently corrupting. One could fight the enemy or one could join the enemy, but one could not do both. To expect to use political methods to abolish political domination was a dangerous delusion.', 'In opposition to both statism and Marxism, Bakunin presents in broad outline the principles of “anarchy,” as he calls what we would today term anarchism, and the anarchist society of the future.
