Based on the provided context, Karl Marx's view of historical necessity in Grundrisse contrasts with Mikhail Bakunin's view of historical development in Statism and Anarchy.

Marx views history as driven by economic conditions and material forces. In Grundrisse, Marx argues that the development of the forces of production and the relations of production are central to historical progress. He sees capital as a contradictory force that both reduces necessary labor time and increases surplus labor, but ultimately aims to expand the productive forces of society. Marx believes that the reduction of necessary labor time is a necessary condition for the free development of individualities, which would allow more time for artistic, scientific, and other pursuits.

In contrast, Bakunin in Statism and Anarchy criticizes Marx's focus on economic preconditions for revolution. Bakunin argues that "Will, not economic conditions, is the basis of his social revolution." He believes that political domination can persist even after economic conditions have changed, suggesting that historical development is not solely driven by economic factors but also by will and other non-economic factors.

Therefore, while Marx sees history as driven by economic forces and material conditions, Bakunin emphasizes the role of will and other non-economic factors in historical development.
reference: In Grundrisse, Marx analyzes historical development through the material accumulation of fixed capital and general social intellect, showing how objective production forces increasingly bring social life under rational control. In Statism and Anarchy, Bakunin rejects preordained historical destinies or abstract laws, maintaining that history is shaped by the concrete struggles of living people striving for liberty and material well-being against state authority. While Marx emphasizes the objective material development of productive forces and intellect, Bakunin stresses active human agency and anti-authoritarian struggle as the primary drivers of history.

The national catechisms of different countries may differ on secondary points, but there are certain fundamental points which must be accepted by the national organizations of all countries as the basis of their respective catechisms, These points are:

Rejecting the principle of imposed and regimented unity, it will be directed from the bottom up, from the circumference to the center, according to the principles of free federation. Its free individuals will form voluntary associations. its associations will form autonomous communes, its communes will form autonomous provinces, its provinces will form the regions, and the regions will freely federate into countries which, in turn. will sooner or later create the universal world federation.

the little tract belongs rather to the standpoint of the eighteenth

We have repelled energeticly every alliance with bourgeois politics, even of the most radical nature. It has been pretended, foolishly and slanderously, that we repudiated all such Political connivance because we were indifferent to the great question of Liberty, and considered only the economic or material side of the problem. It has been declared that, consequently, we placed ourselves in the ranks of the reaction. A German delegate at the Congress of Basle gave classic expression to this view, when he dared to state that, who ever did not recognise, with the German Socialists Democracy, “that the conquest of political rights (power) was the preliminary condition of social emancipation,” was, consciously or unconsciously an ally, of the Ceasars!

These critics greatly deceive themselves and, “consciously or unconsciously,” endeavour to deceive the public concerning us. We love liberty much more than they do. We love it to the point of wishing it complete and entire. We wish the reality and not the fiction. Hence we repel every bourgeois alliance, since we are convinced that all liberty conquered by the aid of the bourgeoisie, their political means and weapons, or by an alliance with their political dupes, will prove profitable for Messrs. the bourgeois, but never anything more than a fiction for the workers.', 'It is not true then to say that we treat politics abstractly. We make no abstraction of it, since we wish positively to kill it. And here is the essential point upon which we separate ourselves absolutely from politicians and radical bourgeois Socialists (now functioning as social or radical democracy which is only a facade for capitalistic democracy,). Their policy consists in the transfor- mation of State politics, their use and reform. Our policy, the only policy we admit, consists in the total abolition of the State, and of politics, which is its necessary manifestation.

It is only because we wish frankly to this abolition of the State that we believe that we have the right to call ourselves Internationalists and Revolutionary Socialists; for whoever wishes to deal with politics otherwise than how we do; whoever does not, like us, wish the total abolition of politics, must necessarily participate in the politics of a patriotic and bourgeois State. In other words, he renounces, by that very fact, in the name of his great or little national State, the human solidarity of all peoples, as well as the economic and social emancipation of the masses at home.', 'Messrs. the bourgeois of all parties, including the most advanced, however cosmopolitan they are, when it is a question of gaining money by a more and more extensive exploitation of the labour of the people, are all equally fervent and fanatical in their patriotic attachment to the state. Patriotism is in reality, nothing but the passion for and cult of the national State, as M. Thiers, the very illustrious assassin of the parisian proletariat, and the present saviour of France, has said recently. But whoever says “State” says domination; and whoever says “domination” says exploitation. Which proves that the popular or “folk’s” State, now become aud unhappily remaining today the catchword of the German Socialist Democracy, is a ridiculous contradiction, a fiction, a falsehood, unconscious on the part of those who extol it, doubtlessly, but, for the proletariat, a very dangerous trap.

These “Letters to a Frenchman” were not actually addressed to anyone in particular, but were merely the form the author used to indicate the informality and personal quality of what he had to say.

This long extract naturally divides itself into three distinct sections: a)

His
Letters to a Frenchman
are among the most important of Bakunin’s writings. For it is in this major work that Bakunin made his unique contributions to the theory and practice of revolution. It was written during the stormy period of the Franco-Prussian War when France faced certain defeat. The government of Napoleon III had collapsed and the succeeding provisional republican government was hopelessly demoralized. The French armies were in full retreat and the Prussian troops were at the gates of Paris. It was in the midst of this crisis that Bakunin developed ideas which have since become the watchwords of libertarian revolutionary movements and to which even the authoritarians still pay lip service — ideas such as turning the wars between states into civil wars for the Social Revolution; the people-in-arms fighting a guerrilla war to repulse a foreign army and simultaneously defending the revolution against its domestic enemies; all power to the grass-roots organizations spontaneously created by the revolution; a federalist alternative to centralized statist revolution-by-decree, among others.', 'As I have already said, I am not at all alarmed by the platonic attachment of the peasants to the Emperor [Napoleon III]. This attachment is merely a negative expression of their hatred for the landed gentry and the bourgeois of the cities; it need not seriously hinder the development of the Social Revolution.

The last principal grievance of the city proletariat against the peasants concerns their avarice, their unbridled egoism, and their fanatical commitment to the individual ownership of land. Workers who reprimand the peasants for all these faults should first reflect and ask themselves: who is not an egoist? Who in present society is not avaricious, in the sense that he holds on passionately to the little property that he has been able to scrape together, so that he and his loved ones shall not die of hunger and privation in the economic jungle of this merciless society? It is true that the peasants are not communists. They hate and fear those who would abolish private property, because they have something to lose — at least, in their imagination, and imagination is a very potent factor, though generally underestimated today. The vast majority of the city workers, owning no property, are immeasurably more inclined towards communism than are the peasants. Nothing is more natural; the communism of the one is just as natural as the individualism of the other, but this is no reason to praise the workers for their communist inclinations, nor to reproach the peasants for their individualism. Such sympathies are merely a superficial manifestation of deep socialist sentiments, distorted by ignorance and the malevolent propaganda of the exploiters; a rash of measles, which will yield to the determined treatment of revolutionary socialism. The peasants will donate neither their land nor their money nor their lives just to keep Napoleon III on his throne; but they are willing to kill the rich and to take and give their property to the Emperor because they hate the rich in general. According to the provided context, Karl Marx's description of the Paris Commune in "The Civil War in France" and Mikhail Bakunin's principles in "The Program of the International Brotherhood" present contrasting views on the state and its role in revolution.

Marx describes the Paris Commune as an example of the "Dictatorship of the Proletariat," which he sees as a necessary step towards a stateless society. He notes that the Commune's actions, such as organizing large-scale industry, were moving towards communism, which is the direct antithesis of Proudhon's individualist socialism. Marx emphasizes that the state is inherently a tool of class oppression and that the working class must dismantle it as part of their struggle for freedom.

In contrast, Bakunin's "Program of the International Brotherhood" explicitly rejects any idea of dictatorship and a controlling power. He advocates for a revolutionary alliance that excludes any form of state control or directive power. Bakunin's vision is one where the people themselves are the revolutionary force, and he sees revolutions as arising from the deep consciousness of the masses rather than being orchestrated by individuals or secret societies. He calls for the destruction of property and the state, advocating for a society organized by the collective property of federated workers' associations.

Thus, while Marx sees the Commune as a step towards a stateless society through the dictatorship of the proletariat, Bakunin's program envisions a revolution that avoids state control entirely, focusing on the direct action and organization of the working class.
reference: In The Civil War in France, Marx details how the Paris Commune dismantled standing state forces like the army and police, replacing them with accountable municipal councillors elected by universal suffrage who were subject to short-term recall. In The Program of the International Brotherhood, Bakunin outlines a revolutionary alliance that explicitly rejects dictatorial or directive state power, acting instead as a non-coercive organ within popular anarchy. Both authors prioritize dismantling conventional standing state armies and centralized command structures, though Marx focuses on representative municipal accountability while Bakunin emphasizes informal organization within popular anarchy.

According to the context provided, Mikhail Bakunin's concept of "natural obedience" in "God and the State" contrasts sharply with John Stuart Mill's account of moral sanction in Utilitarianism.

Bakunin argues that the belief in God and divine authority leads to the establishment of hierarchical structures and the oppression of humanity. He states that "With the name of God they imagine that they can establish fraternity among men, and, on the contrary, they crush and degrade us. For with God come the different degrees of divine inspiration; humanity is divided into men highly inspired, less inspired, uninspired. All are equally insignificant before God, it is true; but, compared with each other, some are greater than others; not only in fact — which would be of no consequence, because inequality in fact is lost in the collectivity when it cannot cling to some legal fiction or institution — but by the divine right of inspiration, which immediately establishes a fixed, constant, petrifying inequality. The highly inspired must be listened to and obeyed by the less inspired, and the less inspired by the uninspired. Thus we have the principle of authority well established, and with it the two fundamental institutions of slavery: Church and State."

On the other hand, John Stuart Mill in Utilitarianism, discusses the possibility of moral sanctions for utilitarianism. He notes that utilitarianism can have both external and internal sanctions. External sanctions include "the hope of favour and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe, along with whatever we may have of sympathy or affection for them or of love and awe of Him, inclining us to do His will independently of selfish consequences." Mill suggests that these external sanctions, including religious motivations, can be applied to utilitarianism just as they are to other moral systems.

Thus, while Bakunin sees divine authority as a means of oppression and hierarchy, Mill sees it as a potential source of moral sanction for utilitarianism, provided it is not the only source and is balanced with other considerations.
reference: In God and the State, Bakunin defines human liberty as voluntary obedience to natural laws that an individual personally recognizes as true, rejecting all external impositions from divine or human authorities. In Utilitarianism, Mill locates the ultimate moral sanction in an internal, subjective feeling in human minds rather than external coercion or command. Both authors locate genuine moral obligation and freedom within internal individual recognition rather than external decree, though Bakunin frames this as recognizing natural laws while Mill defines it as an internal subjective feeling for moral utility.

Karl Marx's distributive principle in the Critique of the Gotha Programme and John Stuart Mill's view of proportional remuneration in Principles of Political Economy present contrasting approaches to economic and social organization.

### Karl Marx's Distributive Principle

In the Critique of the Gotha Programme, Marx outlines a distributive principle that contrasts sharply with the prevailing capitalist system. Marx argues that in a future communist society, distribution should be based on the principle "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs." This principle is a significant departure from the capitalist system, which is based on the exchange of labor for wages.

Marx's distributive principle is rooted in the idea of a classless society where the means of production are collectively owned. He argues that the distribution of goods and services should be based on need rather than the ability to pay or the amount of labor contributed. This is a radical departure from the capitalist system, which Marx sees as inherently exploitative, where the value of labor is determined by the market and not by the actual needs of the workers.

### John Stuart Mill's View of Proportional Remuneration

In Principles of Political Economy, John Stuart Mill discusses the concept of proportional remuneration, which is a more moderate and gradual approach to economic reform. Mill advocates for a system where wages are based on the value of the labor performed, but he does not propose a complete overhaul of the capitalist system. Instead, he suggests that wages should be proportional to the amount of labor contributed, reflecting the idea of fair compensation.

Mill's view is more aligned with the existing capitalist framework, where wages are determined by supply and demand, and labor is valued based on its productivity. He does not advocate for the nationalization of the means of production or the abolition of private property, which are central to Marx's vision of communism.

### Key Differences

1. **Economic System**:
   - **Marx**: Advocates for a classless society with collectively owned means of production.
   - **Mill**: Supports a modified capitalist system with some reforms, such as fair wages based on labor contribution.

2. **Distribution of Goods**:
   - **Marx**: Distribution based on need, ensuring that everyone receives according to their needs.
   - **Mill**: Distribution based on the value of labor, reflecting a more equitable but still market-driven system.

3. **Role of the State**:
   - **Marx**: Calls for the state to nationalize the means of production and control the distribution of goods.
   - **Mill**: Sees the state as a regulator of the economy, ensuring fair wages and conditions, but not necessarily nationalizing all means of production.

4. **Social Justice**:
   - **Marx**: Seeks to eliminate class distinctions and ensure that everyone's basic needs are met.
   - **Mill**: Aims for a more just and equitable society, but still within the framework of a market economy.

In summary, Marx's distributive principle in the Critique of the Gotha Programme represents a radical transformation of the economic and social order, while John Stuart Mill's view of proportional remuneration in Principles of Political Economy represents a more moderate reform within the existing capitalist framework.

response:
According to Bakunin's vision in "Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism," his approach contrasts with Marx and Engels' centralized plan in the following ways:

1. **Federalism vs. Centralization**: Bakunin advocates for federalism, which he sees as a decentralized form of organization where power is distributed among local communities and associations. He criticizes the state and advocates for a society organized by free associations. In contrast, Marx and Engels propose a centralized form of production and state control over the economy, as seen in their emphasis on the need for a proletarian revolution that would lead to the abolition of private property and the establishment of a state that would wither away.

2. **Role of the State**: Bakunin is explicitly anti-statist, viewing the state as an instrument of oppression. He believes that the state should be abolished and replaced by a confederation of autonomous communities. Marx and Engels, while critical of the existing state, envision a transitional state that would eventually wither away after the establishment of a classless society.

3. **Economic Organization**: Bakunin's socialism is based on the spontaneous action of free associations, operating according to the laws of social economy without governmental regulation. Marx and Engels, on the other hand, propose a planned economy under the control of the state, where the means of production are owned collectively but managed by the state.

4. **Critique of Authoritarian Socialism**: Bakunin criticizes the authoritarian socialism of figures like Cabet, Louis Blanc, the Fourierists, and the Saint-Simonists, who sought to impose their vision of a socialist society through state power. He contrasts this with his own vision of a society organized by free, voluntary associations.

These differences highlight the fundamental contrast between Bakunin's anarchist federalism and the Marxist vision of a centralized, state-controlled socialist society.
reference: In Federalism, Socialism, Anti-Theologism, Bakunin demands that collective property and society be organized strictly from below upward through voluntary associations, warning that state authority converts socialism into slavery. In the Manifesto of the Communist Party, Marx and Engels argue that the proletariat must use state power to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the state organized as the ruling class. While Bakunin insists on total anti-authoritarian decentralization, Marx and Engels prioritize state-directed economic centralization to expand productive forces.

response:
John Stuart Mill and Mikhail Bakunin have fundamentally different views on the nature and efficacy of universal suffrage and representative government.

Bakunin criticizes universal suffrage as an illusion, arguing that it does not lead to genuine freedom or the will of the people. He points out that in practice, the ruling class, typically the bourgeoisie, maintains control over the government despite the formal equality of the representative system. Bakunin believes that the people, who are often uneducated and busy with work, cannot effectively supervise their representatives, leading to a fiction of popular control. He also notes that those in power, whether legislators or executives, tend to view the governed with a sense of superiority, leading to a natural conflict of interests.

In contrast, Mill defends the idea that universal suffrage can lead to a more representative government. He argues that if all adults had the right to vote, the influence of the majority would be decisive, and the need for secrecy in voting would be lessened. Mill believes that public opinion would be the ultimate power, and that the ballot should be used to ensure that the will of the people is expressed. He suggests that even if all were educated and had votes, the ballot would still be necessary to ensure that public duties are performed honestly and openly.

Thus, while Bakunin sees universal suffrage as a deceptive and ineffective mechanism for genuine democracy, Mill sees it as a means to ensure that the government truly represents the will of the people.
reference: In Considerations on Representative Government, Mill describes representative democracy as the ideally best government form because it vests ultimate sovereignty in all citizens and encourages civic participation through public functions. In The Illusion of Universal Suffrage, Bakunin counters that voting within an economically unequal society is a total illusion that briefly flatters workers before returning them to economic servitude. While Mill views electoral participation as an indispensable tool for civic development and governance, Bakunin contends that political voting without prior economic equality merely masks ongoing class subjection.

According to Marx's characterization in Capital, Volume 1, capital accumulation can occur without a previous increase in the quantity of capital, challenging the traditional view that production must precede accumulation. Marx criticizes John Stuart Mill for his simplistic view that profit arises from the productivity of labor, stating that Mill confounds the duration of labor-time with the duration of its products. Marx argues that this view leads to the erroneous conclusion that the more durable the product, the greater the profit, which is not necessarily true.

In contrast, John Stuart Mill, as described in his Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy, views profit as arising from the productive power of labor. He states that if laborers produce a surplus-value of 20%, the profit will be 20% of the total wages, which Marx characterizes as tautological and false. Mill also discusses the idea that the gains from foreign trade are not due to a "general glut" but rather from the employment of capital that would otherwise yield no profit, a view Marx criticizes as oversimplified.

Marx's critique of Mill highlights the limitations of viewing profit solely through the lens of labor productivity and the need to consider the dialectical relationship between capital and labor. Marx emphasizes the contradictions within bourgeois economic thought, particularly the evasion of the origin of surplus-value, which Mill, in Marx's view, fails to adequately address.

In Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy, Mill argues that profit arises from the productive power of labor itself rather than exchange incidents. Although both locate profit in productive labor rather than market trading, Marx emphasizes the parasitic extraction of labor power by capital, whereas Mill presents profit as the natural return to labor's inherent productive capacity.

Society, far from decreasing his freedom, on the contrary creates the individual freedom of all human beings. Society is the root, the tree, and liberty is its fruit. The materialistic. realistic, and collectivist conception of freedom, as opposed to the idealistic, is this: Man becomes conscious of himself and his humanity only in society and only by the collective action of the whole society. He frees himself from the yoke of external nature only by collective and social labor, which alone can transform the earth into an abode favorable to the development of humanity. Without such material emancipation the intellectual and moral emancipation of the individual is impossible. He can emancipate himself from the yoke of his own nature, i.e. subordinate his instincts and the movements of his body to the conscious direction of his mind, the development of which is fostered only by education and training. But education and training are preeminently and exclusively social ... hence the isolated individual cannot possibly become conscious of his freedom.

The freedom of other men, far from negating or limiting my freedom, is, on the contrary, its necessary premise and confirmation. It is the slavery of other men that sets up a barrier to my freedom, or what amounts to the same thing, it is their bestiality which is the negation of my humanity. For my dignity as a man, my human right which consists of refusing to obey any other man, and to determine my own acts in conformity with my convictions is reflected by the equally free conscience of all and confirmed by the consent of all humanity. One can distinguish the main elements in the attainment of freedom. The first is eminently social. It is the fullest development of all the faculties and powers of every human being, by education, by scientific training, and by material prosperity; things which can only be provided for every individual by the collective, material, intellectual, manual, and sedentary labor of society in general.

He frees himself from the yoke of external nature only by collective and social labor, which alone can transform the earth into an abode favorable to the development of humanity.', '<2-hop: Karl Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy> The mode of production of material life conditions the general process of social, political and intellectual life. It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness.']
response:
Bakunin and Marx have different perspectives on human self-consciousness and freedom, as reflected in their respective works.

Bakunin argues that human self-consciousness and freedom are realized through collective social action. He states, "Man completely realizes his individual freedom as well as his personality only through the individuals who surround him, and thanks only to the labor and the collective power of society." For Bakunin, freedom is a social construct that emerges from the interactions within society. He emphasizes that "The freedom of other men, far from negating or limiting my freedom, is, on the contrary, its necessary premise and confirmation."

In contrast, Marx's materialist conception of history posits that human consciousness and social relations are determined by material conditions. Marx writes, "The process of social, political and intellectual life is altogether necessitated by the mode of production of material life"; and "it is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness." Marx's view suggests that the material conditions of life, such as the mode of production, shape human consciousness and social relations.

While Bakunin sees freedom as a collective achievement, Marx views consciousness as a product of material conditions. Bakunin's account is more focused on the social and collective aspects of freedom, whereas Marx's materialist proposition emphasizes the economic and material base that underpins social relations and consciousness.
reference: In Man, Society, and Freedom, Bakunin maintains that individual human consciousness and liberation from nature develop exclusively through collective social labor within society. In A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, Marx asserts his core historical materialist thesis that social existence determines human consciousness, with material production conditioning social and intellectual life. Both thinkers reject idealist notions of isolated individual consciousness, agreeing that human awareness and emancipation are fundamentally rooted in collective material existence.

We accept all natural authorities and all influences of fact, but none of right; for every authority or every influence of right, officially imposed as such, becoming straight away an oppression and a falsehood, would inevitably impose upon us, as I believe I have sufficiently shown, slavery and absurdity.

In short, we reject all legislation, all authority, and every privileged, licensed, official, and legal influence, even that arising from universal suffrage, convinced that it can only ever turn to the advantage of a dominant, exploiting minority and against the interests of the immense, subjugated majority.

reference_contexts: ['<1-hop: John Stuart Mill, A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive> All inference is from particulars to particulars: General propositions are merely registers of such inferences already made, and short formulæ for making more: The major premiss of a syllogism, consequently, is a formula of this description.', '<2-hop: Mikhail Bakunin, What is Authority?> Does it follow that I reject all authority? Far from me such a thought. In the matter of boots, I refer to the authority of the bootmaker; concerning houses, canals, or railroads, I consult that of the architect or engineer. For such or such a special knowledge I apply to such or such a savant. But I allow neither the bootmaker nor the architect nor the savant to impose his authority upon me.']
response:
According to John Stuart Mill's account in "A System of Logic," he presents general logical premises as the foundation of his work. Mill emphasizes the importance of logic and the scientific method in understanding the world. He views logic as a discipline that can be studied and applied systematically.

In contrast, Mikhail Bakunin's treatment of expert authority in "What Is Authority" is critical. Bakunin rejects the idea of absolute, universal, and infallible authority, whether it be from experts or scientists. He argues that while we should respect the knowledge and experience of experts, we should not accept their authority as absolute or impose it as a right. Bakunin believes that such authority would lead to oppression and slavery.

Therefore, while Mill sees logic as a legitimate and necessary authority in the pursuit of knowledge, Bakunin sees all forms of official authority, including that of experts, as potentially oppressive and detrimental to human liberty.
reference: In A System of Logic, Mill analyzes general premises in logic as provisional registers of past empirical observations from particulars rather than absolute truths. In What is Authority?, Bakunin accepts consulting specialized experts like architects or bootmakers for specific knowledge, but refuses to let any expert impose compulsory authority. Both thinkers reject fixed, infallible dogmas imposed from above—Mill treating logical rules as empirical generalizations, and Bakunin accepting expert knowledge only when consulted voluntarily without coercive authority.

Indeed the source of people’s trouble, lies not in this or that form of government, but in the existence and manifestation of Government itself, whatever form it may assume.

This, finally, is the contradiction, already historic, that exists between the scientific communism developed by the German school and accepted in part by the authoritarian and English socialists on one side, and the Proudhonism, fully developed and pushed to its last consequences, preferred, on the other, by the proletariat of the Latin countries. response:
According to Mikhail Bakunin, the strategy of decreeing social changes through centralized state authority, as advocated by authoritarian communists, differs fundamentally from the theory of spontaneous revolutionary action arising directly from popular initiatives, which is a core tenet of revolutionary or libertarian socialism.

Bakunin criticizes the idea that the social revolution can be decreed and organized by a dictatorship or a Constituent Assembly. He argues that such an approach is fallacious and doomed to failure. Instead, he advocates for a strategy where the revolution is waged and fully developed through the spontaneous and continued mass action of groups and associations of the people. This approach relies on the direct initiative of the workers themselves through their industrial combinations, rather than the direct initiative of the state.

Bakunin believes that no single mind, not even a genius, nor a collective dictatorship of a few supremely endowed individuals, can encompass the infinite multiplicity and diversity of the real interests, aspirations, wills, and needs that constitute the collective will of the people. Therefore, he argues that any attempt to devise a social organization capable of satisfying each and all through centralized authority is impractical and likely to fail.

In contrast, Bakunin emphasizes the importance of the people's own spontaneous actions and the organization of their social and industrial solidarity. He sees this as the only way to achieve a free society, as opposed to the authoritarian approach that seeks to capture and transform society through political power.

It argues that true social transformation must emerge directly from popular deeds and local initiative. According to Bakunin, the concept of an invisible, non-official collective influence guiding popular anarchy differs significantly from an open political party representing the unified historical interests of the working class. Here are the key differences as supported by the context:

1. **Visibility and Official Status**:
   - **Invisible, Non-Official Collective Influence**: Bakunin emphasizes that this form of leadership is "invisible" and "without any official legality and significance." It operates through the natural influence of its members, without seeking or holding any official power or recognition.
   - **Open Political Party**: An open political party, by contrast, would be visible and officially recognized. It would have a formal structure, leadership, and possibly elected representatives.

2. **Purpose and Method**:
   - **Invisible, Non-Official Collective Influence**: This form of leadership aims to influence the people through the "natural, personal influence" of its members. It seeks to guide the spontaneous revolutionary movement of the people towards the organization of popular liberty.
   - **Open Political Party**: An open political party would aim to represent the unified historical interests of the working class more directly. It would likely engage in formal political activities, such as organizing rallies, publishing manifestos, and participating in elections.

3. **Role in Revolution**:
   - **Invisible, Non-Official Collective Influence**: Bakunin suggests that this form of leadership would play a role in leading the revolution, but not by seeking or holding power. Instead, it would act "in defiance of all ambitious persons who are divided and fighting among themselves."
   - **Open Political Party**: An open political party would more directly participate in the political process, potentially seeking to take control of the state apparatus to implement its vision for the working class.

4. **Influence and Power**:
   - **Invisible, Non-Official Collective Influence**: Bakunin argues that this form of leadership is "that much more effective and powerful" because it remains "invisible and unacknowledged." It relies on the collective action and influence of its members among the people.
   - **Open Political Party**: An open political party would rely on formal structures and possibly legal authority to influence the masses. It might seek to gain control of state institutions to implement its policies.

In summary, Bakunin's concept of an invisible, non-official collective influence guiding popular anarchy is fundamentally different from the idea of an open political party representing the unified historical interests of the working class. The former operates through subtle, decentralized influence, while the latter seeks to gain and wield official power and recognition.
reference: One approach proposes a non-official, invisible collective dictatorship consisting of dedicated revolutionaries who exert informal influence during popular anarchy without holding formal political power. On the other hand, the open party model rejects secret sectarian dictates, positioning communist organizers as an explicit section of the broader working-class movement. This party functions publicly to highlight common proletarian interests across national boundaries and guide the historical movement toward class power.

['[5. The Contradiction Between the Productive Forces and the Form of Intercourse as the Basis for Social Revolution]
This contradiction between the productive forces and the form of intercourse, which, as we saw, has occurred several times in past history, without, however, endangering the basis, necessarily on each occasion burst out in a revolution, taking on at the same time various subsidiary forms, such as all-embracing collisions, collisions of various classes, contradiction of consciousness, battle of ideas, etc., political conflict, etc. From a narrow point of view one may isolate one of these subsidiary forms and consider it as the basis of these revolutions; and this is all the more easy as the individuals who started the revolutions had illusions about their own activity according to their degree of culture and the stage of historical development.

Marx argues that these material conditions, which individuals find in existence, are the real basis of historical development and social change. This perspective emphasizes the necessity of material conditions and the contradiction between productive forces and the form of intercourse as the primary drivers of historical change.

While the former highlights structural economic contradictions as the driver of revolution, the latter emphasizes active human consciousness and rebellious instinct.

The critique of wage labor focusing on how money relations disguise unpaid surplus value, as presented in the context from Marx, argues that the capitalist system inherently exploits workers by converting their labor into surplus value that is appropriated by capitalists. This surplus value is generated through the unpaid labor of workers, which is masked by the money relations in the market. According to Marx, this exploitation is a fundamental contradiction of capitalism, where the capitalist appears as the owner of capital, while the worker is merely a wage laborer.

In contrast, the argument that state ownership of capital merely converts the state into a single universal employer, as implied in the context from Marx, suggests that state ownership does not fundamentally alter the nature of exploitation. The state, in this view, would still be the owner of capital, and workers would still be wage laborers. The state would control the means of production, but the relationship between the state and workers would still be one of employer and employee, with the state acting as the sole employer. This would not eliminate the exploitation of labor, as the state would still appropriate the surplus value generated by the labor of its workers.

Both critiques highlight the persistence of exploitation under different forms of ownership. The first critique focuses on the individual capitalist exploiting workers, while the second critique suggests that state ownership does not fundamentally change the exploitative relationship, as the state would still control the surplus value produced by labor.
reference: The economic critique of the wage system demonstrates how monetary remuneration creates an illusion where all labor appears fully compensated, thereby masking the extraction of unpaid surplus labor by private capital. Conversely, the political critique focuses on the structural coercion of wage dependence, arguing that transferring property to state control does not eliminate exploitation. It contends that making the state the sole capitalist and landlord merely replaces private masters with a single universal state master, leaving workers in continuous servitude.

['In human society, as in nature, every being lives only by the supreme principle of the most positive intervention in the existence of every other being. And when we demand the freedom of the masses, we do not even dream of obliterating any of the natural influences that any individual or group of individuals exercise upon each other. If the Church and the State were private institutions, we would, no doubt, be against them, but we would not contest their right to exist. We fight them because they are organized to exploit the collective power of the masses by official and violent superimposition. If the International were to became a State we, its most zealous champions, would become its most implacable enemies.', 'The object of this Essay is to assert one very simple principle, as
entitled to govern absolutely the dealings of society with the
individual in the way of compulsion and control, whether the means used
be physical force in the form of legal penalties, or the moral coercion
of public opinion. That principle is, that the sole end for which
mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with
the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. That
the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any
member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to
others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient
warrant. He cannot rightfully be compelled to do or forbear because it
will be better for him to do so, because it will make him happier,
because, in the opinions of others, to do so would be wise, or even
right. These are good reasons for remonstrating with him, or reasoning

independence is, of right, absolute. Over himself, over his own body and
mind, the individual is sovereign.', 'But, I repeat, the revolt of the individual against society is much more difficult than revolt against the State. Freedom, morality, and the human dignity of the individual consists precisely in this; that he does good not because he is forced to do so, but because he freely conceives it, wants it, and loves it.

According to John Stuart Mill in "On Liberty," society may only restrict individual action to prevent harm to others. This view contrasts with Mikhail Bakunin's critique of the state, as expressed in multiple passages, which argues that any state apparatus inherently negates human morality and enforces collective submission.

Mill asserts that the sole purpose for which society can interfere with an individual's liberty is to prevent harm to others. He states, "The only part of the conduct of any one, for which he is amenable to society, is that which concerns others. In the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute."

In contrast, Bakunin views the state as an institution that inherently negates human morality and enforces collective submission. Bakunin argues that the state's nature is to impose itself by force, regardless of the good it may command, and that it disrupts the natural and positive mutual intervention between individuals that is essential for human society.

Mill advocates for a representative system where the interests of different social classes are balanced, ensuring that no single class can dominate the government. He suggests that this balance can be achieved through mechanisms like plural voting, where education is given a greater say to counterbalance the numerical weight of the least educated class. Mill believes that such a system, if properly designed, can lead to a more just and equitable representation of the population's interests.

In contrast, Bakunin argues that all political states, including those that claim to represent the people, are inherently mechanisms of class domination. He sees representative systems as a fiction that conceals the true power dynamics, where a small elite controls the state and uses it to maintain their privileges over the majority. The defense of individual self-expression through independent experiments of living, as implied in the context provided, contrasts with the view that human freedom is a collective product realized exclusively through social solidarity in several key ways:

1. **Source of Freedom**: According to the context from Bakunin, human freedom is seen as a collective product that arises from the interdependence and collective action of individuals within society. Freedom is not an individual achievement but a social outcome. In contrast, the independent experiments of living suggest that freedom can be achieved through individual actions and choices, without necessarily relying on or being constrained by societal structures.

He states that "Society, far from decreasing his freedom, on the contrary creates the individual freedom of all human beings." This view contrasts with the idea that individuals can and should experiment with different forms of living independently of societal norms and structures.

This implies that freedom is a communal and reciprocal concept, dependent on the recognition and respect of others. The independent experiments of living, on the other hand, might suggest a more individualistic and self-reliant conception of freedom, where the individual's self-expression is paramount.

4. **Means of Achieving Freedom**: Bakunin argues that freedom is achieved through collective action and the transformation of society, particularly through the organization of workers' councils and the abolition of class distinctions. This collective approach contrasts with the idea of achieving freedom through individual experiments, which might focus more on personal autonomy and self-determination.

According to Marx in "Grundrisse" and "Value Price Profit," the definition of commodity value as the objective embodiment of socially necessary labor time contrasts with the theory that prices fluctuate around production costs governed by supply and demand in several key ways:

1. **Value as Socially Necessary Labor Time**: Marx argues that the value of a commodity is determined by the amount of socially necessary labor time required to produce it. This is an objective measure, independent of market fluctuations. He states that "real value itself – independently of its rule over the oscillations of the market price – in turn negates itself and constantly posits the real value of commodities in contradiction with its own character, that it constantly depreciates or appreciates the real value of already produced commodities."

2. **Price Fluctuations and Supply-Demand**: In contrast, the theory that prices fluctuate around production costs governed by supply and demand suggests that market prices are not fixed but rather move up and down based on the balance between supply and demand. Marx acknowledges that "Supply and demand constantly determine the prices of commodities; never balance, or only coincidentally; but the cost of production, for its part, determines the oscillations of supply and demand." 

3. **Market Price vs. Value**: Marx notes that while market prices may fluctuate, on average, they tend to equilibrate with the values of commodities. However, he argues that profit is derived from selling commodities at their values, not from the prices of commodities. He states, "If you cannot explain profit upon this supposition, you cannot explain it at all."

4. **The Role of Competition**: Marx points out that while competition tends to equalize prices with production costs over time, this is not the primary determinant of value. He writes, "We thus see that the price of a commodity is indeed determined by its cost of production, but in such a manner that the periods in which the rise is compensated for by a fall and the fall by a rise, carry the most frightful devastation in their train, and, like an earthquake, cause bourgeois society to shake to its very foundations."

In summary, while the theory of supply and demand suggests that prices fluctuate around production costs, Marx's view is that the value of a commodity is fundamentally determined by the objective amount of labor time required to produce it, and that profit is derived from selling commodities at their true value, not their market price.

Marx sees this as a form of "workshop despotism," where capitalists exert authority over laborers, reducing them to mere parts of a machine. He also notes that the pressure of competition leads to a constant struggle for survival, which he views as a form of "anarchy in the social division of labour."

In contrast, the defense of economic competition as an indispensable stimulus against human idleness, as seen in the passage from "Poverty of Philosophy," suggests that competition is essential for the "advent of equality" and the "general interest." According to this view, competition drives progress and ensures that individuals pursue their self-interest, which in turn benefits society as a whole. M. Proudhon, as quoted in "Poverty of Philosophy," argues that competition is a form of "industrial emulation" that leads to the "negation of itself" and the "ruin of those whom it drags in its train," but also acknowledges that it is necessary for the development of society.

Marx's critique and Proudhon's defense both recognize the role of competition in economic life, but they differ in their assessment of its overall impact. Marx sees competition as a necessary but inherently contradictory force that leads to exploitation and inequality, while Proudhon views it as a dynamic and progressive mechanism that drives social development and equality.

According to Bakunin in "The Social Revolution," the revolutionary communal model contrasts with representative parliamentary systems in several key ways:

1. **Executive and Legislative Functions**: In the revolutionary communal model, executive and legislative functions are not separated as they are in representative parliamentary systems. Instead, the model advocates for the direct administration of local affairs by the people themselves through assemblies of delegates and their representatives. This contrasts with representative parliamentary systems where these functions are typically separated, with a legislative body (like a parliament) making laws and an executive branch (like a government) implementing them.

2. **Direct Democracy vs. Representative Democracy**: Bakunin describes the revolutionary communal model as a form of direct democracy where the people directly participate in decision-making through assemblies and delegates. This is in contrast to representative parliamentary systems where the people elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf. Bakunin argues that direct democracy allows for more immediate and practical application of the people's will, as opposed to the potential for representatives to misrepresent or ignore the will of the people.

3. **Control and Accountability**: In the revolutionary communal model, there is a strong emphasis on the people's control and accountability over their representatives. Delegates are revocable and bound by formal instructions from their constituents. This is different from representative parliamentary systems where representatives are elected for fixed terms and may not be immediately accountable to their constituents in the same way.

4. **Purpose of Government**: Bakunin views the state as an "excrescence" that should be destroyed, advocating for a system where the few legitimate functions of government are performed by "Communal and thereafter responsible agents." This contrasts with the representative parliamentary systems that aim to protect minority viewpoints and secure expert deliberation, often through complex legislative processes and checks and balances.

5. **Inclusivity and Spontaneity**: The revolutionary communal model emphasizes the spontaneous organization of the people based on their real interests, without the imposition of a preconceived plan. This is different from the representative parliamentary systems that often rely on structured processes and expert deliberation to ensure the protection of minority viewpoints and the quality of legislation.

In summary, the revolutionary communal model seeks to empower the people directly and spontaneously, while representative parliamentary systems aim to balance the interests of different groups through structured representation and deliberation.

For instance, he states that "the ruling ideas of each age have ever been the ideas of its ruling class" and that "ideas, views, and conceptions, in one word, man’s consciousness, changes with every change in the conditions of his material existence, in his social relations and in his social life."

In contrast, the view that moral sentiments and intellectual ideas drive human progress is more aligned with the perspective of Auguste Comte and Positivism as described by Mill in "Auguste Comte and Positivism." Mill argues that feelings and character are more fundamental to social change than ideas. He states, "Ideas do not govern and overthrow the world; the world is governed or overthrown by feelings, to which ideas serve only as guides." According to Mill, the social state and the character of individuals determine what ideas will be current, rather than the other way around.

Thus, while Marx sees economic and material conditions as the primary drivers of historical change and intellectual development, Mill suggests that moral sentiments and character are the primary forces that shape society and ideas.

Conversely, the liberal idealist perspective contends that intellectual discernment, cultivated moral sentiments, and disinterested ideals are the primary forces guiding human progress and shaping political institutions. While the former views ideas as reflections of underlying material class relations, the latter attributes social advancement to the moral and intellectual cultivation of human character.

According to Marx in "Capital Volume 1," the diagnosis of industrial pathology caused by detail specialization is presented as a negative consequence of the division of labor. Marx argues that while the division of labor contributes to the wealth and civilization of society, it also leads to the alienation and degradation of the individual worker. Specifically, Marx states that in manufacture, each laborer is made poor in individual productive powers, becoming a detail laborer whose activity is reduced to mechanical motion. This specialization can lead to the "neglect of the intellectual, social, and martial faculties" of the worker, as well as physical and mental health issues, as evidenced by the "catalogue of labour’s diseases" that has expanded with the advent of modern mechanical industry.

On the other hand, the economic justification of the division of labor as the primary source of wealth and civilization is articulated by Adam Smith and others. Smith, as cited by Marx, argues that the division of labor increases productivity and efficiency, making each worker a cheaper workman. Smith sees the division of labor as a source of social inequalities but still praises its economic benefits. Marx acknowledges Smith's recognition of the social inequalities but emphasizes that the division of labor is a specific form of capitalist production that alienates the worker and devalues their skills over time.

In summary, while the division of labor is economically justified as a means to increase productivity and wealth, Marx diagnoses it as a source of industrial pathology that degrades the worker's skills and health. The two perspectives contrast in their focus: the economic justification highlights productivity gains, whereas the diagnosis of industrial pathology focuses on the negative social and health impacts on the individual worker.
reference: The critical analysis of industrial manufacturing diagnoses the detailed division of labor as a form of human crippling, arguing that confining a worker to a single monotonous operation attacks the individual at the roots of life and mutilates human capacity. Conversely, the classical economic analysis defends the division of labor as the indispensable foundation of civilization, asserting that separating employments increases productive power and generates the material wealth required for social progress. While the former highlights the psychological and physical degradation of the worker under specialized manufacture, the latter emphasizes the collective economic productivity enabled by specialized labor.

According to Marx in "Capital Volume 1," industrial capitalism transforms the traditional family by integrating women and children into the social production process. Marx argues that this integration of women into the workforce, alongside the exploitation of children, creates a new economic foundation for gender relations. He states that the old family ties are torn apart by modern industry, and the family is reduced to a mere instrument of production. This transformation is seen as a step towards a higher form of the family and relations between the sexes, but in its current capitalist form, it is described as a source of corruption and slavery.

In contrast, in the "Manifesto," Marx critiques the traditional family as a school of patriarchal despotism. He argues that bourgeois marriage is a system of wives in common, and the family is used by the ruling class to maintain control over the working class. The family, as it exists under capitalism, is seen as a means of exploiting women and children, and the Communists aim to abolish it as part of their broader critique of capitalist exploitation.

Thus, while both texts critique the traditional family, they do so from different perspectives. Marx in "Capital Volume 1" focuses on the economic transformation brought about by industrial capitalism, whereas in the "Manifesto," he critiques the family as an institution that serves the interests of the ruling class.
